examples.professional: The core sample shows a transition from arenaceous sandstone to dark shale, which tells us the water depth changed.
examples.analytical: Arenaceous deposits often record ancient river or beach environments, so geologists classify them carefully before drawing conclusions about past climates.

nuance.analogy: Arenaceous is like a field guide label for sand: the same grainy material you know from the beach, named in the careful language of rock classification.
nuance.etymology: From Latin arenaceus, meaning sandy, from arena, meaning sand.
common_mistakes: Stressing the first syllable, as in AR-en-AY-shus, instead of the syllable NAY.
Confusing arenaceous with arena, the stadium, because the two words share the same root.

senses.definition: In an aromatic manner.
senses.example: an aromatically spiced Indian dish

core.definition: In a way that has a strong, pleasant smell, especially of spices, herbs or flowers.

pronunciation.tip: The main stress falls on MAT, the third syllable. The final -ly is a light 'lee' sound, and the middle vowel is a reduced 'uh'.

nuance.connotation: Positive. It suggests a pleasant, rich scent, often of cooking or gardens.
nuance.usage_note: Americans rarely use this adverb in conversation. They prefer phrases like 'smelled really good' or 'smelled of spices.' You are more likely to meet it in food writing, nature writing or product descriptions, so recognize it there rather than forcing it into everyday speech.

distinctions.note: Fragrantly is similar but more poetic; aromatically often suggests spices or herbs, such as a dish simmering.
Pungently suggests a sharp, strong smell that can be unpleasant, while aromatically is usually pleasant.

examples.professional: The sample blends were tested to see how they perform aromatically, not just visually.
examples.analytical: The poem describes the garden aromatically, evoking memory through scent rather than sight.

nuance.analogy: Like a room that tells its story through smell before you see anything in it.
nuance.etymology: From aromatic, from Greek aroma (spice), plus the adverb suffix -ally.
common_mistakes: Using aromatically in casual speech where 'with a nice smell' sounds more natural.
Putting the stress on the first syllable instead of MAT.

senses.definition: Clothing and ornamentation; raiment.
senses.example: The actors changed into elaborate array before stepping onto the royal stage.

senses.definition: A collection laid out to be viewed in full.
senses.example: A dazzling array of handmade jewelry filled the tables at the craft fair.

senses.definition: An orderly series, arrangement or sequence.
senses.example: The numbers were printed in an array from smallest to largest.

senses.definition: Order; a regular and imposing arrangement; disposition in regular lines; hence, order of battle.
senses.example: drawn up in battle array

senses.definition: A large collection.
senses.example: We offer a dazzling array of choices.

senses.definition: A matrix.
senses.example: In linear algebra, she multiplied the coefficient array by the input vector.

senses.definition: Any of various data structures designed to hold multiple elements of the same type; especially, a data structure that holds these elements in adjacent memory locations so that they may be retrieved using numeric indices.
senses.example: The function stores each sensor reading in a fixed-size array for fast access.

senses.definition: A ranking or setting forth in order, by the proper officer, of a jury as impaneled in a cause; the panel itself; or the whole body of jurors summoned to attend the court.
senses.example: The clerk prepared the array of jurors before the judge called the trial.

senses.definition: A group of hedgehogs.
senses.example: We saw a prickly array of hedgehogs snuffling through the garden at dusk.

senses.definition: A microarray.
senses.example: The lab processed the microarray to measure gene expression across all samples.

senses.definition: A militia.
senses.example: The rebels assembled an array of local militia in the valley.

senses.definition: To clothe and ornament; to adorn or attire.
senses.example: He was arrayed in his finest robes and jewels.

senses.definition: To lay out in an orderly arrangement; to deploy or marshal.
senses.example: The general arrayed his troops along the ridge before dawn.

senses.definition: To set in order, as a jury, for the trial of a cause; that is, to call them one at a time.
senses.example: The judge arrayed the panel of jurors before the trial began.

core.definition: A wide, impressive range of things; in math and computing, an ordered grid of values in rows and columns.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on RAY, the second syllable, which rhymes with 'day' and 'say'. Do not stress the first syllable as AR-ay, and keep the r clear.

nuance.connotation: Positive in ordinary use, suggesting variety and abundance; neutral and technical in computing.
nuance.usage_note: Americans say 'an array of options' in writing and speech for a wide selection, such as 'an array of cheeses.' In math and programming, an array is a structured list, often indexed by position, such as a NumPy array. For the verb, 'arrayed' is the common past participle, as in 'arrayed in a row.' It works in both casual and formal use.

distinctions.note: Arrangement is the act or result of putting things in order; array usually emphasizes an impressive display or a set of values.
Range is a general word for variety; array often suggests a larger, more showy set.
In programming, an array has fixed, indexed elements of one type, while a list may grow and may hold mixed types depending on the language.

examples.everyday: The bakery had an amazing array of pastries, so I couldn't pick just one.
examples.professional: The model takes a NumPy array of pixel values as input, so we need to check the shape before training.
examples.analytical: The essay offers an array of examples, but it never explains why they belong to the same argument.

nuance.analogy: An array is like a parking garage: each space has a fixed row and column, so you can find any car by its position.
nuance.etymology: From Old French arei, 'order, arrangement,' related to arrayer, 'to arrange'.
common_mistakes: Stressing the first syllable as AR-ay
Using array for a single item or small set, when selection or variety is more natural
Assuming arrays in programming behave the same way as lists in every language

array.etymology: From Middle English *arrayen*, from Anglo-Norman *arraier* (compare, *areer* (“to put in order”)), from Vulgar Latin **arrēdō* (“to put in order, arrange, array”), from **rēdum* (“preparation, order”), from **raid* or **raidā* (“preparation, order”) or…

senses.definition: Constructed with one or more pivoted joints which allow bending of an otherwise rigid structure.
senses.example: The articulated arm of the robot reaches around obstacles on the assembly line.

senses.definition: Of a vehicle, composed of component parts each with its own wheels and chassis, e.g. an articulated lorry, articulated bus, or certain kinds of streetcars and trains.
senses.example: The articulated bus navigated the tight downtown turns without scraping the curb.

senses.definition: Qualified by an article.
An articulated vehicle, such as a locomotive.
senses.example: The transit authority ordered three new articulateds for the busiest routes.

core.definition: Built from sections joined by a hinge or pivot so it can bend, like an articulated bus or truck.

pronunciation.tip: The stress falls on TIK, and the r is pronounced. The -ate syllable is 'lay' and the ending is a short 'tid', not 'ated' with a long vowel.

nuance.connotation: Neutral. It describes a physical design and carries no emotional tone.
nuance.usage_note: In American English, an articulated bus is common among transit agencies, and a long truck with a hinged trailer is usually called a semi or tractor-trailer. Articulated lorry is a British term. The word also describes clearly expressed ideas, though that use is less common than the mechanical sense.

distinctions.note: Jointed is a general word for anything with joints, while articulated suggests a specific design with sections that pivot.
Articulate describes clear speech or writing, while articulated describes physical structure.
Flexible describes something that bends easily, while articulated describes a design that bends at specific hinges.

examples.everyday: I took the articulated bus downtown because it was so crowded, and it turned the corners really smoothly.
examples.professional: The fleet team wants to replace the older rigid buses with articulated models on the busiest routes.
examples.analytical: The engineer argued that an articulated design improves turning radius but adds maintenance demands at the hinge.

nuance.analogy: Like an elbow, it bends at a joint but stays connected as one piece.
nuance.etymology: From Late Latin articulatus, from Latin articulare, to divide into joints.
common_mistakes: Using articulated to mean well spoken; the usual American word for that is articulate.
Saying 'articulated lorry' in the US, where people would say semi or tractor-trailer for the truck.

senses.definition: Significant artistic skill.
senses.example: Her artistry with watercolors earned her a scholarship to the state's most respected art institute.

core.definition: Great skill and creativity in making art or in performing a craft with expressive beauty.

pronunciation.tip: Stress the first syllable. The 'tr' blends into a clear 'tree' sound with an r. Don't stress the last syllable or add an extra vowel, as in 'ar-TIS-tuh-ree'; the ending is one unstressed 'ree.'

nuance.connotation: Positive. It praises skill and creativity, often in performance, cooking, design, or sports.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use artistry to compliment skill that feels creative and beautiful, such as a chef's knife work or a pitcher's control. It is somewhat elevated, so in casual talk you might say 'she's amazing at this' instead. It works well in reviews, speeches, and compliments like 'That was pure artistry.'

distinctions.note: Art is the broad category of creative work; artistry is the skill and personal touch that a maker brings to it.
Craftsmanship emphasizes technical quality and precision; artistry adds creativity and expressive beauty.
Technique is the method; artistry is how skillfully and creatively the technique is used.

examples.everyday: That pitch was pure artistry; I've never seen anyone curve a ball like that.
examples.professional: The design team's artistry shows in the logo, but the new layout also has to work well on phones.
examples.analytical: Critics often separate a painter's technical artistry from the emotional meaning of the work, yet the two are hard to disentangle.

nuance.analogy: Artistry is the difference between a pitch that is accurate and one that is a joy to watch.
nuance.etymology: From artist plus -ry; artist ultimately from Latin ars 'skill, art'.
common_mistakes: Stressing the second syllable, as in 'ar-TIS-tree,' or adding an extra syllable at the end.
Using artistry for ordinary art objects; it refers to the skill and quality of the maker, not the work itself.

senses.definition: The attribute of being entirely self-derived, in contrast to being derived from or dependent on another; the quality of having within oneself the entire reason for one's being; utter independent self-existence and self-sustenance.
senses.example: Theologians describe God's aseity as the self-existence that depends on nothing else.

core.definition: In theology, the quality of God existing in and from himself, depending on nothing outside himself for his existence.

pronunciation.tip: The stress falls on SEE, and the final syllable is a light 'tee.' The middle syllable is a short 'ih,' not a long ee. Don't say it as 'ay-SEE-ity' with a long first vowel.

nuance.connotation: Neutral and technical; used with reverence in theology.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use 'aseity' almost only in theology, philosophy, and academic discussions of divine attributes. It is rarely used outside seminary or philosophy classes. In everyday speech people would say 'self-existence' or 'independence' to express a similar idea.

distinctions.note: 'Self-existence' is the more general phrase in English, while 'aseity' is the technical theological term for God's independence.
'Eternity' refers to existence without beginning or end, while 'aseity' emphasizes that God's existence does not depend on anything else.

examples.everyday: My seminary friend explained that God's aseity means he doesn't need anything, so he's never in want.
examples.professional: In the systematic theology course, we studied aseity as the first attribute that distinguishes God from all created things.
examples.analytical: Classical theists argue that divine aseity requires God to be pure actuality, because anything dependent would have a cause outside itself.

nuance.analogy: Aseity is like a light source that shines by its own power, while the moon only reflects light it receives from elsewhere.
nuance.etymology: From Latin a se, 'from oneself,' with the English suffix -ity.
common_mistakes: Pronouncing it with a long first vowel as 'ay-SEE-ity'; the first vowel is a short schwa or 'uh.'
Using 'aseity' for ordinary independence in people; it is a technical term for God's self-existence.
nuance.biblical_note: No single Hebrew or Greek word means aseity, but the idea is grounded in Scripture. Exodus 3:14 reveals the divine name 'I AM WHO I AM,' which points to God's self-existence. John 5:26 says the Father has life in himself and has granted the Son to have life in himself. Acts 17:25 says God is not served by human hands as though he needed anything, which supports the idea that God depends on nothing.

aseity.etymology: From Medieval Latin *aseitas* (“state of being by itself”), from Classical Latin *a se* + *-itas*.

senses.definition: Made from the wood of the ash-tree.
senses.example: An ashen bow and quiver of arrows beside.

senses.definition: Of or resembling ashes.
senses.example: A fine, ashen dust hung in the air.

senses.definition: Ash-colored; pale; anemic.
senses.example: His ashen face belied his claims of good health.

senses.definition: Appalled; upset.
To turn into ash; make or become ashy.
To make or become pale.

core.definition: Very pale and grayish in color, usually because of shock, fear, illness, or extreme tiredness.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on the first syllable, ASH, and the second syllable is a weak uh. Do not pronounce it as ay-shen, and do not confuse it with ashy, which describes dry skin or a dusty surface.

nuance.connotation: Negative. It usually describes someone who looks pale and unwell, often from fear, shock, or illness.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use ashen in storytelling, news descriptions, and everyday talk about someone who looks suddenly pale. It is more vivid than pale and sounds a bit dramatic in ordinary speech. A natural comment on someone who looks this way is to ask whether they are okay.

distinctions.note: Pale is the everyday word for light skin color, while ashen suggests a grayish, lifeless paleness caused by shock or illness.
Ashy usually describes dry, grayish skin or something covered in ash, while ashen describes a face or complexion drained of color.

examples.everyday: She went ashen when the doctor called her name, and I thought she was going to faint.
examples.professional: When the finance lead saw the revised numbers, he went ashen and asked for the report again.
examples.analytical: The novel's ashen landscapes and drained colors mirror the moral exhaustion of its postwar characters.

nuance.analogy: An ashen face is like a fireplace after the fire has gone out: the warmth and color are gone, leaving only gray.
nuance.etymology: From ash, the tree or the residue of burning, plus the suffix -en, meaning made of or resembling.
common_mistakes: Confusing ashen with ashy, which has a different meaning and usually describes dry skin.
Using ashen for ordinary light skin color, where pale would be more natural.

ashen.etymology: From Middle English *aschen*, *asshen*, from Old English *æsċen* (“made of ashwood”), equivalent to *ash* + *-en*.

senses.definition: Confrontational; tending or seeming to assault; characterized by assault.
senses.example: an assaultive patient; an assaultive incident

senses.definition: A person who assaults others.
senses.example: The guard was an assaultive man who picked fights and threatened anyone who questioned him.

core.definition: Tending to attack others, physically or verbally; aggressive or confrontational in behavior.

pronunciation.tip: The stress is on SAWL, with the l silent, and the final syllable is a short 'tiv'. Learners often add a full vowel after the l, but the word has only two main syllables after the stress.

nuance.connotation: Negative. It describes aggressive or threatening behavior, and in clinical or correctional settings it is a neutral but serious term.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use assaultive mainly in medical, psychiatric, correctional, and legal writing, such as describing a patient or inmate who has been violent. In everyday talk, people say aggressive, violent, or hostile. Avoid it in casual speech, because it sounds technical.

distinctions.note: Aggressive is everyday and can describe mere assertiveness, while assaultive means tending to physically or verbally attack others.
Violent describes force in general, while assaultive focuses on a tendency to attack another person.

examples.everyday: My neighbor's dog became really assaultive when someone came near its yard, so we keep it inside now.
examples.professional: The shift report flagged the patient as assaultive, so staff decided to increase supervision for the evening.
examples.analytical: The debate's tone turned assaultive when speakers used personal attacks rather than arguments about policy.

nuance.analogy: An assaultive person is like a boxer who keeps swinging even when the match has already been decided.
nuance.etymology: From assault, with the adjective suffix -ive.
common_mistakes: Using it as a casual synonym for angry, which sounds too technical.
Confusing assaultive with assertive, which is positive and means confident.
Pronouncing the l in the stressed syllable.

senses.definition: Capable of being assigned (all senses).
senses.example: In many programming languages, numeric values are not assignable to string variables.

senses.definition: Capable of being specified or shown.
senses.example: The bug was assignable to a single misconfigured environment variable.

core.definition: Able to be assigned to a person, task or category, or able to be identified and specified as a cause.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on the SY syllable, and the final -able is reduced to a syllabic l, so say it as buhl rather than ah-bul. Many non-native speakers stress the last syllable by mistake.

nuance.connotation: Neutral; it is a precise descriptive word with no emotional charge.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use assignable mostly in business, legal, quality-control and software contexts, as in assignable cause or assignable fields. In everyday speech they say can be assigned or can be given. It sounds stiff in casual conversation.

distinctions.note: Assignable describes what could be assigned; assigned describes what has already been given to someone.
Appointable refers to a person who can be given a position; assignable covers tasks, rights and causes as well.

examples.everyday: The landlord says the rent increase isn't assignable to anything specific, so I asked for a breakdown.
examples.professional: The engineers found an assignable cause for the defect: a worn tool on line three.
examples.analytical: Philosophers ask whether moral responsibility is always assignable to a single agent inside complex institutions.

nuance.analogy: Like a seat number on a ticket, an assignable item can be given to one specific person or place.
nuance.etymology: From Anglo-French assigner, 'to allot', from Latin assignare, 'to mark out to'.
common_mistakes: Stressing the final syllable instead of the SY syllable.
Using assignable in casual talk where can be given or can be assigned sounds more natural.

senses.definition: To authenticate by means of belief; to surmise; to suppose to be true, especially without proof.
senses.example: We assume that, as her parents were dentists, she knows quite a bit about dentistry.

senses.definition: To take on a position, duty or form.
senses.example: Mr. Jones will assume the position of a lifeguard until a proper replacement is found.

senses.definition: To adopt a feigned quality or manner; to claim without right; to arrogate.
senses.example: He assumed an air of indifference.

senses.definition: To receive, adopt (a person).
senses.example: The childless couple chose to assume the orphaned boy as their own son.

senses.definition: To adopt (an idea or cause).
senses.example: The new director quickly assumed the cause of reducing emissions across all plants.

core.definition: To accept or suppose that something is true without proof; or to take on a role, duty or responsibility.

pronunciation.tip: The stress falls on the second syllable, and the ss is a plain /s/. The vowel is the long oo sound, so say 'uh-SOOM' and not 'uh-SYOOM', which is a British-influenced variant.

nuance.connotation: Neutral; it can sound presumptuous if you assume something without checking, especially about someone else.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use 'assume' in everyday speech, as in 'I assume you want the usual' or 'I assumed you knew'. In casual talk people often say 'I'm guessing' or 'I figured', but 'assume' is always standard. Use 'I assume' for reasonable guesses, and say 'I know' or 'I checked' when you have evidence.

distinctions.note: Presume is more formal and often suggests a reasonable basis or a legal presumption, while assume is the everyday word for supposing.
Suppose is softer and common in phrases like 'I suppose so', while assume is firmer and often treats the supposition as a working belief.
Guess implies uncertainty or a rough estimate, while assume implies you have taken something as the basis for further reasoning.

examples.everyday: I assume you want the usual, so I'll order it for you.
examples.professional: I'm going to assume the migration finishes on Friday unless someone tells me otherwise.
examples.analytical: Locke's argument assumes that personal identity follows memory, a premise that critics have questioned.

nuance.analogy: Like filling in a blank on a form with a plausible guess and then building on it; the structure stands only as long as the guess holds.
nuance.etymology: From Latin assumere 'to take up, take to oneself', from ad 'to' plus sumere 'to take'.
common_mistakes: Using 'assume' for a fact you have verified; use 'know' or 'confirm' when you have evidence.
Pronouncing it 'uh-SYOOM' with a y sound, which is a British-influenced variant; Americans say 'uh-SOOM'.

assume.etymology: From Latin *assūmō* (“accept, take”), from *ad-* (“to, towards, at”) + *sūmō* (“take up, assume”).

senses.definition: With speed; quickly; rapidly.
Courant, in full chase: running, at full stride with its legs in the air.
senses.example: The greyhound raced after the rabbit at speed, legs stretched out across the open field.

core.definition: Moving or working quickly; at high speed or a fast pace.

pronunciation.tip: Stress the long e in 'speed', and keep 'at' weak. Keep the sp cluster clean, and do not insert an extra vowel like 'es-peed'.

nuance.connotation: Neutral. It can sound positive when describing efficiency or alarming when describing danger, depending on context.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use 'at speed' more in technical, driving, sports or news contexts, as in 'The truck was going at speed when it hit the guardrail' or 'The software processes data at speed.' In casual talk people more often say 'fast' or 'at full speed'. It is common but a little formal in tone. A natural reply is 'Wow, that's fast.'

distinctions.note: Quickly describes how fast something happens without emphasizing high speed, while at speed emphasizes moving or working at high velocity.
At full speed is more intense and implies maximum capacity, while at speed can describe a less extreme fast pace.

examples.everyday: The kids were riding their bikes down the hill at speed, and I got nervous.
examples.professional: The new cluster processes millions of records at speed, which cut our reporting time in half.
examples.analytical: Systems that operate at speed often trade interpretability for throughput, a tension worth examining carefully.

nuance.analogy: Like a train that never slows through the station: everything rushes past the window.
nuance.etymology: From Old English 'spēd', meaning success or prosperity, later meaning rapidity of movement.
common_mistakes: Saying 'in speed' instead of 'at speed'.
Using 'with speed' as a direct replacement; 'at speed' is the idiom for fast movement, while 'with speed' is more common in writing.

senses.definition: That attend or attends; that is or are in attendance; attendant.
senses.example: The attending guests signed the register before the ceremony began.

senses.definition: Serving on the staff of a teaching hospital as a doctor.
senses.example: The attending physician reviewed the resident's notes before discharging the patient.

senses.definition: Attendant, concomitant.
senses.example: Fear and relief were attending emotions as the results came in.

senses.definition: A physician on the staff of a hospital, especially the principal one that supervises a patient's care.
senses.example: She's an attending in gastroenterology at Mass General.

core.definition: A senior physician on a hospital staff who is formally responsible for supervising a patient's care.

pronunciation.tip: The stress falls on TEN. The -ing ending is a short 'ih' sound plus 'ng', not a long 'ee', so say uh-TEN-ding, not uh-TEN-deeng.

nuance.connotation: Neutral; the word signals seniority and authority in a medical setting.
nuance.usage_note: In American teaching hospitals, the attending is the senior doctor who supervises residents and medical students and takes final responsibility for a patient. Residents often say 'my attending wants to see the scans' in shop talk. Outside medicine, the noun is rarely used, and the adjective meaning 'present' is formal and uncommon.

distinctions.note: A resident is a doctor in training; the attending is a fully licensed senior physician who supervises the resident.
A fellow is a doctor doing advanced subspecialty training; an attending has completed training and supervises patients.
A consultant is called in for advice on a case; the attending is responsible for a patient's ongoing care in a teaching hospital.

examples.everyday: My brother is a resident, and he's always nervous before he presents to his attending.
examples.professional: The attending physician must co-sign the discharge summary before the patient can leave the unit.
examples.analytical: Medical education depends on the attending's dual role as clinician and teacher, whose judgment the resident is trained to internalize.

nuance.analogy: The attending is like a head coach who is accountable for every play, even when the assistant coaches call them.
nuance.etymology: From the verb attend, 'to care for' or 'be present'; the medical sense comes from the phrase attending physician.
common_mistakes: Using attending for any teacher or boss; in medicine it means a senior hospital doctor.
Mispronouncing the -ing as 'een', as in 'uh-TEN-deen'.
Confusing attending with attendant, which means an assistant or aide, not a supervising doctor.

senses.definition: Enthusiastic; keen; eager; showing great interest in something or desire to do something.
senses.example: an avid fan of 1960s sci-fi movies

senses.definition: Greedy.
senses.example: The avid miser counted his coins again and again, never satisfied with what he had.

core.definition: Very eager and enthusiastic about something, especially a hobby, sport, or activity you do often.

pronunciation.tip: The stress falls on the first syllable, and the first vowel is the short a of 'cat.' Learners often say 'AY-vid' with a long a, which sounds like a different word.

nuance.connotation: Positive. It describes a person with strong, sustained interest, and it is almost always used approvingly.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use avid in everyday conversation and in writing, especially with hobbies, sports, reading, and fandom, as in 'She's an avid runner.' It sounds natural and a little enthusiastic, so it fits casual talk as well as writing. It is less common with abstract ideas, where interested or passionate would often sound more natural.

distinctions.note: Eager often describes wanting to do something soon or right now, while avid describes a sustained, ongoing enthusiasm for a subject or activity.
Keen is a little more general and can mean sharp or quick as well as enthusiastic, while avid focuses on a strong, habitual appetite for something.
Fanatical suggests extreme or excessive enthusiasm that may seem unreasonable, while avid is positive and does not imply excess.

examples.everyday: My dad is an avid golfer, so he watches every tournament on TV.
examples.professional: We need an avid beta tester who will report bugs every single day.
examples.analytical: Avid engagement with the sources is required before any sound interpretation can be attempted.

nuance.analogy: An avid fan is like someone who never misses a game and knows every player's stats.
nuance.etymology: From Latin avidus, 'eager, greedy,' from avere, 'to crave.'
common_mistakes: Using 'avid of' instead of 'avid for' or 'avid about,' as in 'an avid of reading.'
Saying 'an avid' with a long a, which changes the word's sound entirely.

avid.etymology: From French *avide*, from Latin *avidus* (“eager, desirous; greedy”), from *aveō* (“wish, desire, long for, crave”).

senses.definition: Of or pertaining to the festival of Bacchus, relating to or given to reveling and drunkenness.
senses.example: Our Bacchanalian dinner party went on until dawn, with wine flowing freely and everyone dancing.

senses.definition: Of or resembling wild or unrestrained revelry.
A bacchanal; a drunken reveler.
senses.example: The hotel bar filled with loud bacchanalians celebrating the team's championship late into the night.

core.definition: Relating to wild, drunken revelry; describing a party or mood of riotous, unrestrained drinking and indulgence.

pronunciation.tip: The stress falls on NAY, the third syllable, and the final -ian is a light, unstressed syllable, not 'ee-an'. The initial Bacch- is pronounced like 'back', with a hard k sound.

nuance.connotation: Mostly negative, suggesting excess and loss of control, though it can be used lightly and playfully for a lively party.
nuance.usage_note: You will mainly see this word in books, articles and sophisticated speech, for example describing a wild night of partying. Americans rarely use it in casual talk and would more often say 'wild' or 'out of control.' Use the adjective; the noun 'bacchanal' is rare and literary.

distinctions.note: Rowdy describes noisy, disorderly behavior in general, while bacchanalian implies drink-fueled, sensual excess and is more literary.
Debauched describes a person who is morally corrupted by dissipation, while bacchanalian describes an event or mood of festive indulgence.

examples.everyday: The Halloween party at Mike's turned into a bacchanalian mess by midnight, so I left early.
examples.professional: The product launch got a little bacchanalian, so HR asked us to keep the next offsite more low-key.
examples.analytical: Nietzsche often contrasts the Apollonian order of art with the bacchanalian frenzy that threatens to dissolve individual identity.

nuance.analogy: Like a dorm party where all the ordinary rules of life have been temporarily suspended.
nuance.etymology: From Latin bacchanalis, from Bacchus, the Roman god of wine, from Greek Bakkhos.
common_mistakes: Pronouncing the initial Bacch- as 'batch' instead of 'back'.
Using bacchanalian as a noun for a person; in everyday speech the adjective describes events and moods, and 'bacchanal' is the rare noun.

senses.definition: At or near the rear.
senses.example: Go in the back door of the house.

senses.definition: Returned or restored to a previous place or condition.
senses.example: He was on vacation, but now he’s back.

senses.definition: Not current.
senses.example: I’d like to find a back issue of that magazine.

senses.definition: Situated away from the main or most frequented areas.
senses.example: They took a back road.

senses.definition: In arrears; overdue.
senses.example: They still owe three months’ back rent.

senses.definition: Moving or operating backward.
senses.example: back action

senses.definition: Pronounced with the highest part of the body of the tongue toward the back of the mouth, near the soft palate (most often describing a vowel).
senses.example: The vowel of lot has a back vowel in most dialects of England.

senses.definition: To or in a previous condition or place.
senses.example: He gave back the money.

senses.definition: In a direction opposite to that in which someone or something is facing or normally pointing.
senses.example: Someone pushed me in the chest and I fell back.

senses.definition: In a direction opposite to the usual or desired direction of movement or progress, physically or figuratively.
senses.example: Wind the film back a few frames.

senses.definition: Towards, into or in the past.
senses.example: These records go back years.

senses.definition: Away from someone or something; at a distance.
senses.example: Keep back! It could explode at any moment!

senses.definition: Away from the front or from an edge (of something or someone).
senses.example: Sit all the way back in your chair.

senses.definition: So as to shrink, recede or move aside, or cause to do so.
senses.example: This tree is dying back.

senses.definition: In a manner that impedes.
senses.example: Fear held him back.

senses.definition: In a reciprocal manner; in return.
senses.example: If you hurt me, I’ll hurt you back.

senses.definition: Earlier, ago.
senses.example: We met many years back.

senses.definition: To a later point in time. See also put back.
senses.example: The meeting has been moved back an hour. It was at 3 o’clock; now it's at 4 o’clock.

senses.definition: The rear of the body, especially the part between the neck and the end of the spine and opposite the chest and belly.
senses.example: Could you please scratch my back?

senses.definition: The spine and associated tissues.
senses.example: I hurt my back lifting those crates.

senses.definition: Large and attractive buttocks.
senses.example: Those jeans really show off your back, and everyone at the party noticed.

senses.definition: The part of a piece of clothing which covers the back.
senses.example: I still need to finish the back of your dress.

senses.definition: The backrest, the part of a piece of furniture which receives the human back.
senses.example: Can you fix the back of this chair?

senses.definition: That which is farthest away from the front.
senses.example: He sat in the back of the room.

senses.definition: The side of any object which is opposite the front or useful side.
senses.example: Turn the book over and look at the back.

senses.definition: The edge of a book which is bound.
senses.example: The titles are printed on the backs of the books.

senses.definition: The side of a blade opposite the side used for cutting.
senses.example: Tap it with the back of your knife.

senses.definition: The reverse side; the side that is not normally seen.
senses.example: I hung the clothes on the back of the door.

senses.definition: Area behind, such as the backyard of a house or the rear storeroom of a retail store.
senses.example: We’ll meet out in the back of the library.

senses.definition: The part of something that goes last.
senses.example: The car was near the back of the train.

senses.definition: The upper part of a natural object which is considered to resemble an animal’s back.
senses.example: The small boat raced over the backs of the waves.

senses.definition: A support or resource in reserve.
senses.example: Our donors were a solid back, ready to cover costs if grants fell through.

senses.definition: The roof of a horizontal underground passage.
senses.example: The miners reinforced the back of the tunnel with steel supports after the rockfall.

senses.definition: Effort, usually physical.
senses.example: Put some back into it!

senses.definition: A non-alcoholic drink (often water or a soft drink), to go with hard liquor or a cocktail.
senses.example: Could I get a martini with a water back?

senses.definition: Among leather dealers, one of the thickest and stoutest tanned hides.
senses.example: The tannery sold heavy back hides to saddle makers who needed the thickest leather.

senses.definition: Clipping of backstroke.
senses.example: She swam the back in under 27 seconds at the regional meet.

senses.definition: A large shallow vat; a cistern, tub, or trough, used by brewers, distillers, dyers, picklers, gluemakers, and others, for mixing or cooling wort, holding water, hot glue, etc.
senses.example: The brewer stirred the wort in the back, cooling it before adding yeast.

senses.definition: A ferryboat.
senses.example: We crossed the river on the back, a small ferry that carried cars and bicycles.

senses.definition: The inside margin of a page.
senses.example: Print the pages so the text stays clear of the back, the inner margin near the binding.

senses.definition: In some team sports, a position behind most players on the team.
senses.example: The backs were lined up in an I formation.

senses.definition: The keel and keelson of a ship.
senses.example: The ship’s back broke in the pounding surf.

senses.definition: To go in the reverse direction.
senses.example: The train backed into the station.

senses.definition: To support.
senses.example: I back you all the way.

senses.definition: To push or force backwards.
senses.example: to back oxen

senses.definition: To make a back for; to furnish with a back.
senses.example: to back books

senses.definition: To adjoin behind; to be at the back of.
senses.example: A narrow garden backs the house, with a fence running along the property line.

senses.definition: To write upon the back of, possibly as an endorsement.
senses.example: to back a letter; to back a note or legal document

senses.definition: To sign or endorse (a warrant, issued in another county, to apprehend an offender).
senses.example: The sheriff in Oregon agreed to back the warrant so local deputies could make the arrest.

senses.definition: To row backward with (oars).
senses.example: to back the oars

senses.definition: To draw from behind the back (a knife etc.) (as also back out).
senses.example: The stranger began to back a knife from behind his jacket as the police approached.

senses.definition: To change direction contrary to the normal pattern; that is, to shift anticlockwise in the northern hemisphere, or clockwise in the southern hemisphere.
senses.example: Meteorologists warned that the wind would back to the southwest by evening, bringing rain.

senses.definition: To brace the yards so that the wind presses on the front of the sail, to slow the ship.
senses.example: The captain ordered the crew to back the main topsail to slow the schooner.

senses.definition: To lay out a second, smaller anchor to provide additional holding power.
senses.example: Worried about the rising gale, the skipper ordered the crew to back their anchor with a second one.

core.definition: To or in the place, position or condition that someone or something was in before; returned to an earlier state.

pronunciation.tip: Use the short vowel of 'cat', not the long vowel of 'bake' or the sound of 'bark'. End with a clear, unvoiced k, with no extra vowel after it.

nuance.connotation: Neutral; the meaning is literal and practical in most uses.
nuance.usage_note: Back is one of the most common words in American speech, used in phrases like 'come back', 'get back', 'call me back' and 'I will be right back.' In phone calls, 'I will call you back' is natural and polite. Americans often prefer 'give it back' to 'return it' in everyday talk, where return sounds formal.

distinctions.note: Return is more formal and often sounds like a written or business word; back is the everyday word in speech.
Backward suggests moving toward the rear or in reverse, or describes a slow or undeveloped condition, while back is the neutral everyday word for returning.

examples.everyday: I will be right back, I just need to grab my wallet from the car.
examples.professional: Can you send the revised deck back to me by Friday?
examples.analytical: Historians warn against reading modern categories back into medieval debates, since those categories were not yet available.

nuance.analogy: Back is like a boomerang: it goes out and then returns to where it started.
nuance.etymology: From Old English bæc, 'back of the body'.
common_mistakes: Saying come back to home instead of come back home.
Using a long vowel, saying bahk instead of the short vowel in BAK.

back.etymology: From Middle English *bak*, from Old English *bæc*, from **bak*, from Proto-Germanic **baką*, possibly from Proto-Indo-European **bʰeg-* (“to bend”).

senses.definition: To regress; to slip backwards or revert to a previous, worse state.
senses.example: He felt better for a little while, before his condition started to backslide.

senses.definition: To shirk responsibility; to renege on one's obligations or commitments.
senses.example: Our treasurer tried to backslide on his promise to repay the club's loan.

senses.definition: To revert back into a life of sin after being saved.
senses.example: After his baptism, Dale began to backslide into the drinking and gambling he had renounced.

senses.definition: A backward regression; a reverting back to a worse state.
senses.example: Her manager was worried by her recent backslide into missed deadlines and sloppy reports.

senses.definition: A dance move in which the feet are alternately slid back and the heels lifted, giving the illusion of walking forwards while actually moving backwards.
senses.example: In the dance class, she practiced the backslide, lifting her heels as she slid back.

core.definition: To slip back into an earlier, worse behavior or condition after having improved or made progress.

pronunciation.tip: Stress the first syllable, BACK, in both the verb and the noun. The second syllable rhymes with 'ride', so do not reduce it to 'slid' with a short i.

nuance.connotation: Negative. It implies a gradual loss of progress, usually through weakness or lack of effort.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use 'backslide' for habits, diets, sobriety, and commitments, as in 'I backslid after two weeks.' It is also common in religious speech for falling away from faith. The word suggests slow slipping rather than a sudden collapse, so it fits better than 'relapse' for ordinary habits. A natural reply is 'Don't worry, just get back on track tomorrow.'

distinctions.note: Relapse usually refers to returning to an illness or addiction and sounds more serious, while backslide is milder and common for everyday habits.
Regress is more formal and technical, often used for development or statistical models, while backslide is informal.

examples.everyday: I quit sugar for a month, but I backslid as soon as the holidays started.
examples.professional: We can't backslide on the security patches we promised the client last quarter.
examples.analytical: Without institutional enforcement, reforms tend to backslide once public attention fades.

nuance.analogy: Like a rowboat drifting back downstream the moment you stop paddling.
nuance.etymology: From back and slide, combining the sense of returning with moving smoothly down or along.
common_mistakes: Using it for a sudden accident; it describes a gradual slipping back.
Saying 'backslided' and 'backslid' inconsistently; 'backslid' is the common past tense in American speech.
Confusing it with 'slide back' in a literal physical sense when the meaning is figurative.

senses.definition: A classical form of dance.
senses.example: a classically-trained ballet dancer

senses.definition: A theatrical presentation of such dancing, usually with music, sometimes in the form of a story.
senses.example: Let's go to the ballet in the theater tomorrow!

senses.definition: The company of persons who perform this dance.
senses.example: Zara joined the ballet at the age of 14.

senses.definition: Any intricate series of operations involving coordination between individuals.
senses.example: Getting the merger approved was a ballet of lawyers, regulators, and accountants moving in perfect coordination.

senses.definition: A light part song, frequently with a fa-la-la chorus, common among Elizabethan and Italian Renaissance composers.
senses.example: The choir sang a madrigal-style ballet with a bouncing fa-la-la refrain during the early music concert.

senses.definition: (uncommon) A (small) ball i.e. roundel on a coat of arms, called a bezant, plate, etc. according to color.
senses.example: The shield displayed three gold ballets on a field of blue, marking the family's ancient lineage.
senses.label: uncommon

senses.definition: To perform an action reminiscent of ballet dancing.
senses.example: The goalie balleted across the crease, leaping and pivoting to block every shot.

core.definition: A classical form of theatrical dance with precise, graceful steps and positions, often performed to music, sometimes telling a story.

pronunciation.tip: The stress falls on the final syllable. The first vowel is a short a, as in 'bat', and the final -et is silent.

nuance.connotation: Positive. Ballet suggests elegance, discipline and artistry, though it can also be used for a complicated situation in a figurative way.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use ballet in everyday speech for lessons, classes and performances, as in taking ballet or going to the ballet. The word refers to the dance form, the performance, or the company, depending on context. Ballet classes are often a childhood activity in American towns, so parents may talk about ballet shoes or recitals.

distinctions.note: Dance is the general word for moving to music, while ballet is one specific classical form with set positions and steps.
Modern dance is looser and less bound by ballet's codified positions, so the two forms look and feel different.
Ballroom dancing is partner dancing for social occasions, while ballet is a theatrical art form usually performed on stage.

examples.everyday: My daughter started ballet class on Saturdays, and she wears her pink shoes everywhere.
examples.professional: Our event planner is booking the ballet company for the donor dinner in March.
examples.analytical: Balanchine's neoclassical ballet demands that the body look effortless while obeying strict geometric lines.

nuance.analogy: Ballet is like a sentence written in a strict grammar, where every movement follows set rules but still expresses feeling.
nuance.etymology: From French ballet, from Italian balletto, a little dance, from ballo 'dance'.
common_mistakes: Pronouncing the final -et, as in BAL-et; the word ends with a vowel sound, ba-LAY.
Stressing the first syllable, which makes the word sound like another English word.

senses.definition: In a condition of bankruptcy; unable to pay outstanding debts or meet financial obligations; specifically, having been legally declared insolvent.
senses.example: a bankrupt merchant

senses.definition: Destitute of, or wholly lacking a good quality, value, etc. one should possess or once possessed.
senses.example: a morally bankrupt politician

senses.definition: To force into bankruptcy.
senses.example: Rising material costs eventually bankrupted the family's small furniture business.

senses.definition: To get placed last in Tycoon with the bankruptcy rule.
senses.example: Thanks to the bankrupt rule, my sister landed in last place in Tycoon again.

senses.definition: One who becomes unable to pay his or her debts; an insolvent person; a bankruptee.
senses.example: The court declared the grocer a bankrupt after his creditors filed suit.

core.definition: Unable to pay debts and legally declared unable to meet financial obligations; also used figuratively to mean completely lacking a good quality.

pronunciation.tip: Stress the first syllable, and say the second syllable with a weak, reduced vowel. Do not add a full vowel as in 'bank-ruh-pit'; the final t is clear but quiet.

nuance.connotation: Negative. It describes financial failure or, figuratively, a serious lack of moral or intellectual value.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use 'bankrupt' for a company or person who has legally filed for bankruptcy or cannot pay debts, often in news or business. In casual speech 'broke' is more common for having little money. The figurative use, such as 'morally bankrupt,' is common in opinion writing and speeches.

distinctions.note: Insolvent is more formal and technical, describing a state of being unable to pay debts, while bankrupt usually refers to a legal status.
Broke is informal and means having no money at the moment, while bankrupt is a serious, often legal, condition.

examples.everyday: After buying that new TV, I'm practically bankrupt until payday.
examples.professional: The supplier went bankrupt last month, so we're switching to a new vendor this quarter.
examples.analytical: A morally bankrupt institution may remain legally solvent, which shows that financial health does not guarantee moral integrity.

nuance.analogy: A bankrupt business is like a bucket with a hole so big that no matter how much water you pour in, it never stays full.
nuance.etymology: From Italian banca rotta, meaning broken bench, from the table of a failed money changer.
common_mistakes: Stressing the second syllable as 'ban-KRUPT'.
Pronouncing the middle vowel fully as 'bank-rup-tent'.
Using 'bankrupt' for simply having little money, when 'broke' is the more natural everyday word.

bankrupt.etymology: from *banca* (“bank”) + *rotto* (“broken, rupted”), which refers to an out-of-business bank, having its bench physically broken, signifying that the working moneylender was insolvent.

senses.definition: To take the wrong approach to a situation; to follow a false lead; to attempt to solve a problem using mistaken assumptions about its true nature.
senses.example: The investigator spent days trying to prove the butler committed the murder, but it turns out he was barking up the wrong tree.

core.definition: To pursue a mistaken idea or approach, or to look for something in the wrong place, and not get the result you want.

pronunciation.tip: Stress the content words 'WRONG' and 'TREE,' and reduce 'up' and 'the' to weak sounds. In quick speech, 'bark up' links into 'bar-kup,' and 'the' sounds like 'thuh.' The w in 'wrong' is silent.

nuance.connotation: Neutral to mildly negative. It suggests a helpful correction more than an insult.
nuance.usage_note: Americans say this in workplaces, school, and everyday conversation to suggest someone is looking in the wrong place. It is friendly when used gently, as in 'If you think the budget is the problem, you may be barking up the wrong tree.' A natural reply is 'Oh, good point. Let me look somewhere else.'

distinctions.note: On the wrong track is a general phrase for a mistaken direction, while barking up the wrong tree suggests a false source or misplaced target.
Off base often means someone is out of line or inaccurate in a statement, while barking up the wrong tree is about pursuing the wrong solution.

antonyms: hit the nail on the head
collocations: if you think that, you're barking up the wrong tree
barking up the wrong tree about the cause
barking up the wrong tree with the vendor

examples.everyday: You think the neighbor's dog is keeping you up, but I think you're barking up the wrong tree, because it's the trash truck.
examples.professional: If you think the latency spike comes from the database, you're barking up the wrong tree; I'd check the load balancer first.
examples.analytical: Her argument assumes that moral failure is the cause of the outcome, and that assumption barks up the wrong tree by ignoring the structural incentives involved.

nuance.analogy: Like a hunting dog barking at the wrong tree while the prey is hiding in another one.
nuance.etymology: An American idiom from the 19th century, based on hunting dogs barking at a tree that does not hold the quarry.
common_mistakes: Using 'on' instead of 'up': it is 'bark up the wrong tree,' not 'bark on the wrong tree.'
Changing it to 'bark at the wrong tree,' which is not the standard idiom.

bark-up-the-wrong-tree.etymology: An allusion to a situation in which a hunting dog misidentifies the tree up which it has chased an animal and positions itself at the base of another tree, barking upward at the branches.

conversation.text: If you think I took your charger, you're barking up the wrong tree.
We were barking up the wrong tree; the bug was in the API, not the database.
Asking Tom for money is barking up the wrong tree. He's broke too.

senses.definition: A round (cylindrical) vessel, such as a cask, of greater length than breadth, and bulging in the middle, made of staves bound with hoops, and having flat ends (heads). The word is sometimes applied to a similar cylindrical container made of metal, usually called a drum.
senses.example: a cracker barrel

senses.definition: Such a cask of a certain size, holding one-eighth of what a tun holds. (See a diagram comparing cask sizes.)
senses.example: The brewer rolled a full barrel of stout into the cellar before the tasting began.

senses.definition: The quantity which constitutes a full barrel: the volume or weight this represents varies by local law and custom.
senses.example: The refinery reported that oil prices had risen to eighty dollars a barrel this morning.

senses.definition: A solid drum, or a hollow cylinder or case.
senses.example: the barrel of a windlass; the barrel of a watch, within which the spring is coiled.

senses.definition: A metallic tube, as of a gun, from which a projectile is discharged.
senses.example: The hunter cleaned the dirt from the rifle barrel before loading a fresh cartridge.

senses.definition: A venturi (in carburetion).
senses.example: The carburetor barrel was clogged with grime, so the engine stalled at idle.

senses.definition: A ceiling-mounted tube from which lights are suspended.
senses.example: A lighting barrel hung from the studio ceiling, carrying spotlights for the evening broadcast.

senses.definition: A wave that breaks with a hollow compartment.
senses.example: Surfers waited for a barrel that would curl over and let them ride inside the wave.

senses.definition: A waste receptacle.
senses.example: Throw it into the trash barrel.

senses.definition: The ribs and belly of a horse or pony.
senses.example: The vet checked the pony's barrel, noting that its ribs and belly were thin after the winter.

senses.definition: The hollow basal part of a feather.
senses.example: Under a microscope, the quill's barrel looked hollow, with a thin shaft that held the vane.

senses.definition: The part of a clarinet which connects the mouthpiece and upper joint, and resembles a barrel.
senses.example: The clarinetist cracked the barrel while assembling the instrument, so she needed a replacement.

senses.definition: Any of the dark-staining regions in the somatosensory cortex of rodents, etc. where somatosensory inputs from the contralateral side of the body come in from the thalamus.
senses.example: Barrels in the rat's somatosensory cortex map each whisker onto a distinct cluster of neurons.

senses.definition: A statistic derived from launch angle and exit velocity of a ball hit in play.
senses.example: His barrel rate climbed this season, as more of his fly balls left the park with ideal launch angles.

senses.definition: To put or to pack in a barrel or barrels.
senses.example: Workers barreled the aged whiskey in oak casks, sealing each one for three years.

senses.definition: To move quickly or in an uncontrolled manner.
senses.example: He came barreling around the corner and I almost hit him.

senses.definition: To assume the shape of a barrel; specifically, of the image on a computer display, television, etc. to exhibit barrel distortion, where the sides bulge outwards.
senses.example: Old television sets often barrel the picture, so the edges of the screen bulge outward.

senses.definition: To bet consecutively on multiple streets.
senses.example: In the poker room, he likes to barrel multiple streets, betting hard on the turn and river.

core.definition: A large, round container with flat ends, usually made of wood or metal, for storing liquids or goods.

pronunciation.tip: Stress the first syllable and make the first vowel a short 'a' as in 'cat'. The second syllable is a weak 'uhl' with no separate 'uh' sound before the l.

nuance.connotation: Neutral. It is a practical, concrete word with no emotional weight.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use barrel for large round containers and also as a unit of measure, especially for oil, where one barrel equals 42 US gallons. For a small metal barrel of beer, people usually say keg. Informally, barrel also means to move very fast, as in barreling down the highway.

distinctions.note: A cask is usually a smaller wooden container, often used for aging wine or whiskey, while a barrel is the more general word.
A drum is usually a metal container for industrial storage, while a barrel can be made of wood or metal.
A keg is a small metal barrel used for beer, and Americans rarely use barrel for a keg in casual talk.

examples.everyday: Can you roll that empty barrel out of the garage before the rain starts?
examples.professional: The refinery shipped two thousand barrels of crude oil to the Gulf terminal this week.
examples.analytical: Oil prices are quoted per barrel because a standard unit makes global comparisons possible.

nuance.analogy: Think of a rain barrel: a round, sturdy container that holds a lot and stays put.
nuance.etymology: From Old French baril, of uncertain origin.
common_mistakes: Spelling it 'barell' with two l's.
Stressing the second syllable as 'bar-REL'.

senses.definition: In a vector space, a linearly independent set of vectors spanning the whole vector space.

A collection of subsets ("basis elements") of a set, such that this collection covers the set, and for any two basis elements which both contain an element of the set, there is a third basis element contained in the intersection of the first two, which also contains that element.
senses.example: The collection of all possible unions of basis elements of a basis is said to be the topology generated by that basis.

senses.definition: A physical base or foundation.
senses.example: Thick concrete piers provide the basis for the bridge's foundation.

senses.definition: A starting point, base or foundation for an argument or hypothesis.
senses.example: Her careful measurements became the basis for our entire argument about the study.

senses.definition: An underlying condition or circumstance.
senses.example: Allow us to compete on an equal basis.

senses.definition: A regular frequency.
senses.example: You should brush your teeth on a daily basis at minimum.

senses.definition: The difference between the cash price a dealer pays to a farmer for his produce and an agreed reference price, which is usually the futures price at which the given crop is trading at a commodity exchange.
senses.example: The corn basis widened this week because local elevators were paying less than futures.

senses.definition: Amount paid for an investment, including commissions and other expenses.
senses.example: Her cost basis in the shares included the brokerage commission she paid in 2015.

senses.definition: 1 2 “basis” listed in the Oxford English Dictionary [2 Ed. 1989]

core.definition: In linear algebra, a set of linearly independent vectors that spans a vector space, so every vector is a unique combination of them.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on the first syllable, and the second syllable is short and unstressed, so avoid BAY-SEES. The plural bases is pronounced BAY-seez, so keep the -s sound distinct when you change the word.

nuance.connotation: Neutral; a precise, technical or formal word with little emotional charge.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use basis constantly in writing and speech, especially in phrases such as on a regular basis, on a case-by-case basis, and on the basis of. In mathematics it names a specific structure, while in everyday talk it means the underlying reason or foundation for a decision. In casual conversation people usually say basics or basically instead.

distinctions.note: Base can mean a physical bottom or a starting point; basis is more abstract, meaning the principle or reason something rests on.
Foundation often sounds concrete or emotional, as in the foundation of a house or a foundation of trust; basis is more analytical and neutral.

examples.everyday: My brother is studying linear algebra, and he keeps saying a basis is the smallest set you need to describe everything.
examples.professional: The model's features form a basis for the feature space, so we can drop the redundant columns.
examples.analytical: A basis of a vector space is a linearly independent spanning set, and the dimension of the space is the number of vectors in any such set.

nuance.analogy: A basis is like a minimal set of primary colors: a few of them, mixed in the right proportions, can produce every shade you need.
nuance.etymology: From Greek basis, meaning step or pedestal, from bainein, to go or step.
common_mistakes: Pronouncing the plural bases as BAY-sess instead of BAY-seez.
Writing on basis of without the article; American English says on the basis of.
Using basis for a physical base, as in the basis of the lamp; say base for physical support.

basis.etymology: From Latin *basis*, from Ancient Greek *βάσις*, from Proto-Indo-European **gʷémtis*, derived from Proto-Indo-European **gʷem-* (whence also *come*).

senses.definition: Synonym of hold a grudge.
senses.example: She has borne a grudge against her brother ever since he sold their father's car.

core.definition: To keep resentment toward someone for a past wrong, refusing to forgive or let it go.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on grudge, which ends with the j sound in judge. The word a is a weak schwa, uh, and bear stays light.

nuance.connotation: Negative, because it implies ongoing resentment and a refusal to forgive.
nuance.usage_note: Americans say bear a grudge or hold a grudge when someone keeps being angry about a past wrong. It is common in everyday speech and sounds mildly critical of the person holding it. A natural reply is Let it go or I'm over it. Use against with the person, as in bear a grudge against him.

distinctions.note: Means the same thing; hold is slightly more common in everyday American speech.
Resent names the bitter feeling itself, while bear a grudge describes keeping that feeling over time.

examples.everyday: She still bears a grudge against her brother for missing her wedding.
examples.professional: I don't bear a grudge about the budget decision; let's focus on what we can change now.
examples.analytical: Moral philosophers often ask whether a person who bears a grudge is justified in keeping resentment, or whether it corrodes their own character.

nuance.analogy: Like carrying a heavy stone in your pocket for years.
common_mistakes: Dropping the article, as in bear grudge; say bear a grudge.
Using for instead of against, as in bear a grudge for him; say bear a grudge against him.
nuance.biblical_note: Scripture warns against holding grudges. Leviticus 19:18 forbids taking vengeance or bearing a grudge against one's own people, and the Hebrew verb behind bearing a grudge, nāṭar, means to keep or preserve. Matthew 6:14-15 teaches that those who forgive others are forgiven by the Father, and Colossians 3:13 urges believers to forgive one another as the Lord has forgiven them.

inflections: born a grudge, borne a grudge

senses.definition: The bell-shaped curve that is typical of the normal distribution.

core.definition: A symmetrical, bell-shaped graph showing a normal distribution, where most values cluster near the average and fewer appear at the extremes.

pronunciation.tip: Both words are stressed on their main syllable, but CURVE is stronger. Say the r in CURVE clearly, and do not turn the vowel into the one in 'cur' or 'curb'.

nuance.connotation: Neutral. It is a descriptive term, though 'on a bell curve' can imply that someone is simply average.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use 'bell curve' in statistics, data science, education and everyday talk about test scores or height. In schools, 'grading on a bell curve' means assigning grades so that most students get middle grades and few get top or bottom grades. In a meeting, 'the bell curve' is fine among technical people, but 'normal distribution' is more precise when you write a report.

distinctions.note: The bell curve is the picture or graph of the distribution, while the normal distribution is the mathematical model and its formal definition.
Gaussian curve is the formal name in mathematics and statistics, named after Carl Friedrich Gauss; 'bell curve' is the everyday name for the same shape.
A skewed distribution has a long tail on one side and its peak is off-center, so it is not a bell curve.

collocations: standard deviation from the bell curve

examples.everyday: My daughter's test scores fell on a bell curve, with most kids in the middle.
examples.professional: Before we set the alert threshold, let's check whether the latency data follows a bell curve.
examples.analytical: Many social phenomena do not produce a bell curve, which is why the normal model can mislead when extreme outcomes matter.

nuance.analogy: Like a hill with most people standing near the top of the slope and fewer at each edge.
nuance.etymology: 'Bell' refers to the shape, which resembles a bell; 'curve' comes from Latin curvus, meaning bent.
common_mistakes: Writing 'bell's curve' with a possessive apostrophe.
Using 'bell curve' to mean a real bell in a sloped line of people, which confuses listeners.
Forgetting that the term is informal, so formal reports should use 'normal distribution'.

senses.definition: Belly flop.
senses.example: The kids giggled as Dad performed a spectacular belly whopper into the pool.

core.definition: A dive or jump into water that lands flat on the stomach or chest instead of entering head or feet first.

pronunciation.tip: Stress BEL in belly and WAH in whopper, and keep the r in whopper. Many Americans pronounce wh as a plain w, so skip the h sound.

nuance.connotation: Neutral to playful. It describes a common pool mishap, often with a laugh and a red stomach afterward.
nuance.usage_note: Americans most often say 'belly flop' for this dive, so 'belly whopper' sounds old-fashioned or regional and may get a smile. You can use it in casual talk with friends or family, but 'belly flop' is the safer choice everywhere. Lifeguards and swim coaches usually say 'belly flop' when warning kids about high dives.

distinctions.note: Same meaning, but belly flop is the everyday American term and is far more common.
A cannonball is a jump with knees pulled up to the chest, and it lands with a big splash; a belly whopper is a flat, stomach-first landing.

collocations: do a belly whopper off the diving board
belly whopper into the deep end

examples.everyday: I tried a flip off the dock and ended up doing a belly whopper, so my stomach is bright red.
examples.professional: Lifeguards should remind kids that a belly whopper from the high board can cause serious injury to the chest and back.
examples.analytical: In diving, a belly whopper is scored poorly not only for the splash but because the body fails to stay straight at entry.

nuance.analogy: Like a sheet of paper dropped flat onto the table instead of sliding in edge first.
nuance.etymology: Belly from Old English belg 'bag'; whopper from whop, 'to strike hard'.
common_mistakes: Using 'belly whopper' in a US pool setting where 'belly flop' is expected, which may confuse listeners.
Confusing it with the Burger King product 'Whopper', which is a hamburger, not a dive.

senses.definition: To cause (something) to change its shape into a curve, by physical force, chemical action, or any other means.
senses.example: If you bend the pipe too far, it will break.

senses.definition: To become curved.
senses.example: Look at the trees bending in the wind.

senses.definition: To cause to change direction.
To change direction.
senses.example: The road bends to the right.

senses.definition: To be inclined; to direct itself.
senses.example: The road bends north past the old mill and follows the river toward town.

senses.definition: To stoop.
senses.example: He bent down to pick up the pieces.

senses.definition: To bow in prayer, or in token of submission.
senses.example: The congregation bent their heads in prayer as the pastor began the blessing.

senses.definition: To force to submit.
senses.example: They bent me to their will.

senses.definition: To submit.
senses.example: I am bending to my desire to eat junk food.

senses.definition: To apply to a task or purpose.
senses.example: He bent the company's resources to gaining market share.

senses.definition: To apply oneself to a task or purpose.
senses.example: He bent to the goal of gaining market share.

senses.definition: To adapt or interpret to for a purpose or beneficiary.
senses.example: Critics accused the senator of bending the data to fit his preferred policy.

senses.definition: To tie, as in securing a line to a cleat; to shackle a chain to an anchor; make fast.
senses.example: Bend the sail to the yard.

senses.definition: To smoothly change the pitch of a note.
senses.example: You should bend the G slightly sharp in the next measure.

senses.definition: To swing the body when rowing.
senses.example: He bent into the oars and pulled hard against the current toward the far shore.

senses.definition: A curve.
senses.example: There's a sharp bend in the road ahead.

senses.definition: Any of the various knots which join the ends of two lines.
senses.example: The sailor tied a sheet bend to join the two ropes before hoisting the sail.

senses.definition: One of the honorable ordinaries formed by two diagonal lines drawn from the dexter chief to the sinister base; it generally occupies a fifth part of the shield if uncharged, but if charged one third.
senses.example: The shield displayed a red bend across a field of gold, a symbol of the family's lineage.

senses.definition: In the leather trade, the best quality of sole leather; a butt; sometimes, half a butt cut lengthwise.
senses.example: The tannery sold only the finest bend leather, cut from the thickest part of the hide.

senses.definition: Hard, indurated clay; bind.
senses.example: Workers dug through a layer of stiff bend until they reached the sandy gravel below.

senses.definition: A severe condition caused by excessively quick decompression, causing bubbles of nitrogen to form in the blood; decompression sickness.
senses.example: A diver who stays deep for too long must ascend very slowly in order to prevent the bends.

senses.definition: The thickest and strongest planks in a ship's sides, more generally called wales, which have the beams, knees, and futtocks bolted to them.
senses.example: The shipwright bolted the new frames to the bend, reinforcing the hull above the waterline.

senses.definition: The frames or ribs that form the ship's body from the keel to the top of the sides.
senses.example: the midship bends

senses.definition: A glissando, or glide between one pitch and another, especially one accomplished by bending a string (such as on guitar).
senses.example: On the recording, she used a bend on the high string to reach the blues note.

core.definition: To curve something or make it change shape or direction, often by pressure or force.

pronunciation.tip: Use the short e of 'bed' and end with a clear d. The n is pronounced before the d, so keep the sound crisp and do not add a vowel.

nuance.connotation: Neutral. The meaning changes with context, such as bending rules, which can sound flexible or unethical.
nuance.usage_note: This is an everyday word for changing shape, such as bending a wire, bending over, or bending the rules. For road curves Americans often say 'curve' or 'turn', though 'bend in the road' is also common. Bend is used for both physical and figurative flexibility.

distinctions.note: Curve describes a shape that is already curved, while bend stresses the change from straight to curved.
Fold means to double something over along a crease, while bend is more general and does not need a sharp crease.
Flex suggests repeated movement back and forth, while bend describes one change of shape.

collocations: bend down to pick something up

examples.everyday: Be careful not to bend the picture frame when you lift it off the wall.
examples.professional: The bracket will bend under heavy load, so we need thicker steel before the next shipment.
examples.analytical: Some philosophers argue that moral principles bend under pressure, but this makes them preferences rather than principles.

nuance.analogy: Like a green branch that gives under the weight of snow rather than snapping.
nuance.etymology: From Old English bendan, meaning to bind or to draw a bow tight.
common_mistakes: Using 'bended' as a past tense; the standard form is 'bent'.
Saying 'bend to down' instead of 'bend down' or 'bend over'.

bend.etymology: From Middle English *benden*, from Old English *bendan* (“to bind or bend, fetter, restrain”), from **bandijan*, from Proto-Germanic **bandijaną* (“to bend”), from Proto-Indo-European **bʰendʰ-* (“to bind, tie”).

senses.definition: Helpful or good to something or someone.
senses.example: Recycling and reusing garbage can be beneficial to the environment.

senses.definition: Receiving a benefit from something.
senses.example: the beneficial owner of a company

senses.definition: Relating to a benefice.
senses.example: The diocese reviewed the beneficial income attached to the parish's clergy positions.

senses.definition: Something that provides a benefit.
senses.example: Free gym access is one beneficial that makes this job worth keeping.

core.definition: Helpful or good for someone or something; producing a useful or positive result.

pronunciation.tip: The primary stress is on FISH, with a light secondary stress on BEN. The -cial ending sounds like 'shul', and the middle vowels are reduced to schwa.

nuance.connotation: Positive. It describes a helpful effect, and it is often used in health, nutrition, and business contexts.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use beneficial in everyday talk about health and habits, such as 'Exercise is beneficial,' and at work when discussing results. It sounds a little formal compared with good for or helpful, but it is completely natural in written and professional speech. The usual structure is beneficial to or beneficial for.

distinctions.note: Advantageous emphasizes a position or edge over others, while beneficial emphasizes good effects in general.
Useful means practical and usable, while beneficial suggests a positive effect on wellbeing or outcomes over time.

examples.everyday: My doctor says walking after dinner is really beneficial for my blood sugar.
examples.professional: The new caching layer has been beneficial to our response times, cutting latency by almost forty percent.
examples.analytical: Mill argued that a policy is beneficial only if its overall consequences increase happiness across the whole society.

nuance.analogy: Something beneficial is like sunlight for a plant: it helps the plant grow without any special effort on its part.
nuance.etymology: From Late Latin beneficialis, from Latin beneficium, 'benefit, kindness'.
common_mistakes: Saying beneficial for a person without a clear object, such as 'It is beneficial me'; say 'beneficial to me' or 'good for me'.
Confusing beneficial with beneficiary, which is a noun for the person who receives a benefit.

beneficial.etymology: From Late Latin *beneficiālis* (“beneficial”), from Latin *beneficium* (“benefit, favor, kindness”).

senses.definition: A descendant of the Biblical Benjamin; one of the tribe of Benjamin.

core.definition: A descendant of Benjamin, the son of Jacob; a member of the tribe of Benjamin in ancient Israel.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on the first syllable, BEN. The middle syllable is a quick 'juh' with a soft j as in 'judge', and the final -ite rhymes with 'light', not with the stressed syllable.

nuance.connotation: Neutral; a precise historical and religious term with no emotional charge.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use this word almost only in religious or historical contexts, such as Bible study, sermons and history classes. Benjamite is a common variant spelling. In everyday talk you would simply say a member of the tribe of Benjamin.

distinctions.note: Benjamin is the name of the youngest son of Jacob; Benjaminite is the name for his descendants or the tribe.
Israelite is the broader term for the people of Israel; Benjaminite picks out one tribe within that people.

examples.everyday: My Bible study group spent the evening talking about Saul, the Benjaminite who became Israel's first king.
examples.professional: In our course on the Hebrew Bible, we map each tribe, including the Benjaminites, to its territory.
examples.analytical: Paul's claim in Philippians 3:5 to be of the tribe of Benjamin shows a pride in ancestry that shapes his identity.

nuance.analogy: Like a family name passed down through generations, Benjaminite marks a line of descent.
nuance.etymology: From Hebrew Binyamin, traditionally 'son of the right hand' or 'son of the south', plus the suffix -ite for a member or descendant.
common_mistakes: Stressing the last syllable as 'ben-juh-min-AITE'.
Confusing Benjaminite (a descendant) with Benjamin (the person).
nuance.biblical_note: The Hebrew name is Binyamin, traditionally read as 'son of the right hand' or 'son of the south'. Genesis 35:18 records that Rachel named him Ben-oni, but Jacob called him Benjamin. Judges 20 describes a war in which the tribe of Benjamin was nearly destroyed. 1 Samuel 9:1-2 introduces Saul, son of Kish, a Benjaminite who became Israel's first king. Philippians 3:5 has Paul state that he is of the tribe of Benjamin.

senses.definition: Search that always expands the option a heuristic rates as most promising.
senses.example: The pathfinding algorithm uses best-first search to explore the most promising routes on the map first.

core.definition: A search method that always expands next the option a heuristic rates as most promising.

pronunciation.tip: The main stress falls on SURCH, with lighter stress on best and first. Americans pronounce the r clearly in first and search, so do not drop it or say 'fist' for first.

nuance.connotation: Neutral. It is a precise technical term with no emotional charge.
