examples.analytical: Such policies, by dispersing authority among rival bodies, enfeeble the state rather than making it stronger.

nuance.analogy: Like a tree whose roots are slowly cut: it still stands, but it has lost the means to hold up in a storm.
nuance.etymology: From Old French enfeblir, from en- (to make) plus feble, feeble.
common_mistakes: Saying FEE-bull with a long i or ending in bell instead of buhl.
Using it for casual weakness; in everyday speech, weaken is more natural.

enfeeble.etymology: From Middle English *enfeblen*, from Old French *enfeblir*.

senses.definition: Fascinated; captivated.

core.definition: Completely fascinated and absorbed, so that you cannot stop paying attention.

pronunciation.tip: The stress falls on the second syllable, -THRALL-. Say the voiceless th with the tongue between the teeth, and the vowel is the open 'aw' sound used in 'caught', which Americans often pronounce the same as 'cot'. The -ed is just a /d/ sound.

nuance.connotation: Positive; it suggests delight and total absorption, though it can also suggest a loss of control.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use enthralled mostly in writing, reviews and descriptions of performances, and it sounds slightly more dramatic than 'fascinated' or 'into it'. In speech you would more often say 'I was totally hooked' or 'the kids were glued to the screen'. The phrases 'enthralled by' and 'enthralled with' are both used, with 'by' a little more common.

distinctions.note: Fascinated is the everyday word for strong interest, while enthralled is stronger and suggests total absorption.
Captivated suggests attraction through charm or beauty, while enthralled suggests being held completely under the spell of something.
Engrossed usually describes concentration on a task, book or problem, while enthralled emphasizes emotional or imaginative fascination.

examples.everyday: The kids were totally enthralled by the magic show, and nobody wanted to leave.
examples.professional: The keynote speaker had the whole room enthralled, so the Q&A session ran long.
examples.analytical: Readers of Dostoevsky are often enthralled by his characters, yet the same intensity can make the moral questions hard to resolve.

nuance.analogy: Like a moth drawn to a lamp: you move toward the light before you decide to.
nuance.etymology: From en- (in) plus thrall, from Old Norse þræll, 'slave, servant'.
common_mistakes: Confusing enthralled with enrolled, which sounds similar but means registered or signed up.
Stressing the first syllable as EN-thralled instead of en-THRAWLD.

senses.definition: Capable of being enumerated; countable.
senses.example: Because the survey responses are finite and enumerable, we can count every one of them exactly.

core.definition: Able to be counted or listed one by one, especially a finite set of items that can be explicitly listed.

pronunciation.tip: The stress falls on 'NOO', the second syllable, and the 'e' after 'm' is a reduced schwa. The final part, '-able', is a weak syllable, so say 'bul' quickly.

nuance.connotation: Neutral. It is a precise word, used in mathematics and formal writing, with no emotional charge.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use enumerable mainly in mathematics, logic and computer science, and in careful academic writing. In everyday speech people say countable, can be counted or can be listed. The word is the opposite of innumerable, which means too many to count, so the two are often confused.

distinctions.note: Countable is the everyday word, while enumerable often implies that the items can be explicitly listed in some order, a stronger condition in mathematics.
Innumerable means too many to count, while enumerable means able to be counted or listed; they are opposites in meaning.

examples.everyday: The reasons he gave for being late were hardly enumerable, so I stopped listening after the third one.
examples.professional: The test set contains a finite, enumerable number of cases, so we can review each one manually.
examples.analytical: A set is enumerable when there exists a function that assigns each of its members a distinct natural number.

nuance.analogy: An enumerable set is like a line of people you can number one by one, even if the line is very long, because every person gets a number.
nuance.etymology: From Latin enumerare, to count out, from e- (out) and numerare (to count), from numerus (number).
common_mistakes: Confusing enumerable (can be counted) with innumerable (too many to count).
Stressing the first syllable, as in EN-yoo-mer-able, instead of ih-NOO-muh-ruh-bul.

senses.definition: Bishops seen as a group.
senses.example: The American Roman Catholic episcopate meets regularly.

senses.definition: The tenure in office of a bishop.
senses.example: Bishop Smith's episcopate ran for more than 30 years.

senses.definition: (rare) A bishop's jurisdiction, the extent of his diocese.
senses.example: The bishop's episcopate stretched across three counties and nearly two hundred parishes.
senses.label: rare

senses.definition: To act as a bishop.
senses.example: For twenty years he episcopated over the northern diocese before retiring quietly.

core.definition: The bishops of a church considered as a group, or the office and term of a bishop.

pronunciation.tip: Stress the second syllable: ih-PIS. The last syllable is reduced to 'pit' (or 'pet'), not 'pate'.

nuance.connotation: Neutral and institutional.
nuance.usage_note: Used in church history and official church documents. 'The American episcopate' means the bishops collectively, while 'during his episcopate' means his time as bishop. The verb sense is very rare.

distinctions.note: Episcopacy more often names government by bishops; episcopate names the bishops as a group or the bishop's term and jurisdiction.
A diocese is the territory a bishop oversees; episcopate can refer to the bishop's authority or tenure.
Hierarchy covers all ranks of clergy; episcopate is only the bishops.

examples.everyday: My friend said the bishop's episcopate lasted twenty years before he retired.
examples.professional: The statement was signed by members of the national episcopate after their annual meeting.
examples.analytical: Cyprian's theology of the episcopate emphasized the unity of the Church around the bishop.

nuance.analogy: Like the word 'judiciary' for judges as a body, and also for a judge's time on the bench.
nuance.etymology: From Late Latin episcopatus, from Greek episkopos, 'overseer.'
common_mistakes: Pronouncing the ending like 'pate' (-payt).
Mixing it up with 'episcopacy' as a system of government.
Using it to mean a single bishop.
nuance.biblical_note: The Greek episkopē ('oversight') appears in 1 Timothy 3:1 (RSV: the office of bishop), and in Acts 1:20 for the office Judas left vacant.

episcopate.etymology: From Late Latin *episcopatus*, from Latin *episcopus*, from Ancient Greek *ἐπίσκοπος* (“watching over”).

senses.definition: The same in one or more respects.
senses.example: We hold that all men are created equal and are thus equal under the law.

senses.definition: The same in value (status, merit, etc): having or deserving the same rights or treatment.
senses.example: We hold that all men are created equal and are thus equal under the law.

senses.definition: The same in all respects that matter practically; interchangeable, fungible, or (even sometimes) identical for practical purposes.
senses.example: Equal conditions should produce equal results.

senses.definition: Exactly identical, having the same value.
senses.example: All right angles are equal.

senses.definition: Adequate; sufficiently capable or qualified.
senses.example: This test is pretty tough, but I think I'm equal to it.

senses.definition: Intended for voices of one kind only, either all male or all female; not mixed.
To be equal to, to have the same value as; to correspond to.
senses.example: Two plus two equals four.

senses.definition: To make equivalent to; to cause to match.
senses.example: David equaled the water levels of the bottles, so they now both contain exactly 1 liter.

senses.definition: To match in degree or some other quality, to match up to.
To have as consequence, to amount to, to mean.
senses.example: Losing this deal equals losing your job.

senses.definition: A person or thing of equal status to others.
senses.example: We're all equals here.

core.definition: Having the same size, amount, value, or status as something or someone else.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on the first syllable, and the second syllable is a weak 'kwul' with no separate vowel. Do not add an extra syllable and say 'ee-kwa-LAY'.

nuance.connotation: Neutral to positive; it often signals fairness, but it can be neutral in measurement.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use equal every day, in math, sports, politics and business, and the word is perfectly neutral. In casual speech people often say 'same' or 'the same amount', but 'equal' is natural in agreements and fairness discussions. When asked how something is split, you can reply 'Equal, please' at a restaurant or among friends.

distinctions.note: Equal means identical in amount or value, while equivalent means similar in effect or value even when the things are not identical.
Same is the everyday word for identical, while equal is more precise and suits measurements, shares, or rights.

examples.everyday: Let's split the bill equal parts, so nobody feels like they paid more.
examples.professional: We want equal access to the dashboard for every team, not just the managers.
examples.analytical: Kant argued that rational beings are equal in dignity, even though they differ in talent and fortune.

nuance.analogy: Like a balanced scale, where both pans carry the same weight.
nuance.etymology: From Latin aequalis 'level, even', from aequus 'equal, level'.
common_mistakes: Saying 'equal with' instead of 'equal to' when you mean matching or being capable: 'I am not equal to this job'.
Adding an extra vowel and saying 'ee-kwa-LAY' instead of the single first-syllable stress.

senses.definition: Suitable for eating; eatable, edible.
senses.example: The guidebook lists which wild plants are esculent and which are toxic.

senses.definition: “Good enough to eat”; attractive.
senses.example: The bakery's cinnamon rolls looked so esculent that I bought three.

senses.definition: Something edible, especially a vegetable; a comestible.
senses.example: The market stalls offered fresh esculents, from sweet corn to young beets.

senses.definition: An edible mushroom.
senses.example: The morel is a prized esculent that grows in spring woodlands.

core.definition: Fit to be eaten; edible. As a noun, it refers to any food item, especially a vegetable.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on the first syllable, 'ES'. The middle syllables are reduced to 'kyuh-luh', and the final 't' is a clear, short sound.

nuance.connotation: Neutral and somewhat technical or old-fashioned; it sounds scholarly rather than everyday.
nuance.usage_note: Americans rarely use 'esculent' in conversation. It appears in botany, cooking history, and older writing. In daily life people say 'edible', 'good to eat', or 'vegetable' instead. Using it with friends would sound like a deliberate choice of an unusual word.

distinctions.note: Edible is the common everyday word, while esculent is more formal or literary and sounds archaic.
Comestible is a formal noun for a food item, while esculent can be an adjective or noun and is more often used for vegetables.

examples.everyday: Some wild mushrooms are esculent, but you should never eat one unless an expert has identified it.
examples.professional: Our menu development team reviewed which esculent plants could be sourced from local farms.
examples.analytical: The essay considers how colonial botanists classified esculent plants according to their nutritional and cultural value.

nuance.analogy: An esculent is like a friendly, approachable item on the menu: it is simply good to eat, without any hidden danger.
nuance.etymology: From Latin 'esculentus', full of food, from 'esca', food.
common_mistakes: Confusing 'esculent' with 'excellent', which is a common error in pronunciation and meaning.
Using 'esculent' in casual speech where 'edible' is the natural word.

esculent.etymology: Latin *ēsculentus* (“fit for eating, eatable, edible; good to eat, delicious; nourishing; full of food”) + *-ent*.

senses.definition: Characteristic of, or pertaining to, an essayist.
senses.example: Her essayistic style wanders through personal memories before arriving at its argument.

core.definition: Relating to an essay or an essayist, especially in being personal, exploratory, and loosely structured.

pronunciation.tip: The main stress falls on the third syllable, IS, and the ending is -ik, not -eek. The middle vowel is a clear ay sound.

nuance.connotation: Neutral. It describes a style of writing rather than judging its quality.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use essayistic mainly in literary criticism, academic reviews, and discussions of writing style. It is rarely used in speech. It usually describes writing that feels personal, reflective, and digressive rather than strictly argumentative.

distinctions.note: Expository writing explains a topic clearly and directly. Essayistic writing can be exploratory, personal, or meandering.
Academic describes scholarly writing in general. Essayistic specifically describes the loose, reflective style of the essay form.

examples.everyday: My book club argued about whether her memoir is too essayistic to count as a novel.
examples.professional: The editor wants the feature article to be less essayistic and more focused on the data.
examples.analytical: Montaigne's essayistic method treats thinking itself as a process of trying ideas, rather than presenting finished conclusions.

nuance.analogy: Essayistic writing is like a walk with a thoughtful friend who stops often to think aloud, rather than a straight road to a destination.
nuance.etymology: From essay, from French essai 'attempt', plus the suffix -istic.
common_mistakes: Stressing the wrong syllable, as in ESS-ay-ISS-tik.
Confusing essayistic with essayist; the first is an adjective and the second a noun for the writer.
Using essayistic to mean short; it describes a style, not length.

senses.definition: To carry out euthanasia on (a person or animal).
senses.example: John decided to euthanize his dying dog.

core.definition: To kill, painlessly and deliberately, an animal (or occasionally a person) to end incurable suffering.

pronunciation.tip: Stress the first syllable, and end with a clear z sound like 'eyes'. Do not copy the stress pattern of euthanasia, which is yoo-thuh-NAY-zhuh.

nuance.connotation: Neutral but clinical and sensitive. It sounds precise and medical, and it can be emotionally heavy when used about a pet or a person.
nuance.usage_note: Americans most often use euthanize in veterinary care, animal shelters and medical or ethical discussions. In casual talk about a pet, people often say put to sleep or put down, which sound gentler. For people, the word is rarely used in everyday American speech, and public debate usually uses terms like medical aid in dying.

distinctions.note: Put down is casual and common in pet owner conversation. Euthanize is formal and clinical, and it is the usual term in veterinary and shelter records.
Kill is direct and general. Euthanize implies a planned, painless death intended to end suffering.

examples.everyday: The vet said his kidneys were failing, so we decided to have him euthanized on Saturday.
examples.professional: Shelter policy requires that we euthanize only animals that are severely ill or unsafe, and only after a documented review.
examples.analytical: The question of whether a physician may euthanize a patient at the patient's request divides ethicists, courts and medical associations.

nuance.analogy: To euthanize is like a careful, humane exit: the goal is to end suffering, not to end a life for convenience.
nuance.etymology: From Greek euthanasia, meaning good death, from eu, good, and thanatos, death.
common_mistakes: Using euthanasia as a verb; the verb is euthanize.
Stressing the -NAY- syllable of euthanasia when saying the verb euthanize, which stresses the first syllable.

senses.definition: The act of eluding or evading or avoiding, particularly the pressure of an argument, accusation, charge, or interrogation; artful means of eluding.
senses.example: His evasion of the question made the committee suspect he was hiding something important.

core.definition: The act of avoiding a question, duty, or responsibility by clever or dishonest means.

pronunciation.tip: The stress is on the second syllable, -VAY-. The -sion ending is pronounced like 'zhun' as in 'vision,' not 'shun.'

nuance.connotation: Negative. It suggests someone is hiding the truth or avoiding responsibility.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use evasion mostly in news, politics, legal settings, and serious discussion of behavior, such as tax evasion or evasion of a question at a press conference. In everyday speech people more often say dodging or getting around the question. Saying someone is 'evading' a topic in casual talk can sound a bit formal.

distinctions.note: Avoidance is a broader, often neutral word for staying away from something, while evasion implies deliberate, sometimes deceptive, dodging.
A lie is a false statement, whereas evasion means avoiding a direct answer without necessarily saying anything false.

examples.everyday: My brother gave a vague evasion when Mom asked why he was late, so she knew something was up.
examples.professional: The manager's evasion of the budget question in the meeting made the team suspicious.
examples.analytical: Her evasion of the moral question suggests that she wants to protect her position rather than examine the argument.

nuance.analogy: Like a fencer stepping quickly aside so the blade never touches them, the speaker moves away from the hard question.
nuance.etymology: From Latin evasio, from evadere, to escape, from e- (out) and vadere (to go).
common_mistakes: Using evasion for a simple, honest refusal; evasion implies deliberate avoidance.
Pronouncing the final syllable as shun instead of zhun.

evasion.etymology: From Middle French *évasion*, from Late Latin *evasionem*.

senses.definition: A beginning.
senses.example: The exordium of the lecture was so brief that we barely noticed it had started.

senses.definition: The introduction to an essay or discourse.
senses.example: The pastor's exordium introduced the sermon's themes before he turned to the scripture reading.

core.definition: The opening or introduction of a speech, sermon or written work, meant to get the audience's attention.

pronunciation.tip: The stress is on ZOR. The ium ending is a weak um, and the dee syllable is clear with a long e. The x sound is a g followed by z.

nuance.connotation: Neutral. It is a technical term in rhetoric and literature, usually used in analysis or teaching.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use exordium mostly in English classes, rhetoric, classics and literary criticism. In everyday speech, people say introduction or opening. You might hear exordium in a sermon or a formal lecture, but it sounds academic and can seem pretentious in casual talk.

distinctions.note: Introduction is the everyday word for the beginning of any talk or text. Exordium is a technical term that refers specifically to the rhetorical opening of a speech or essay.
A prologue is an introductory section of a play, novel or poem that often gives background. An exordium is specifically the rhetorical opening meant to win the audience.

examples.everyday: My professor said the funniest part of the lecture was the exordium, so the rest was a bit dull.
examples.professional: The keynote's exordium was too long, so the audience lost interest before the main point.
examples.analytical: In the classical structure of oratory, the exordium establishes the speaker's credibility and prepares the audience to receive the argument.

nuance.analogy: An exordium is like the opening chords of a song. It sets the tone and invites the audience in before the main melody starts.
nuance.etymology: From Latin exordium, a beginning, from exordiri, to begin a web, from ex- (out) and ordiri (to begin weaving).
common_mistakes: Pronouncing the middle syllable as a long ee, as in eg-ZOR-dee-um, which is actually correct, but many learners stress the dee too much.
Using exordium for a casual beginning of a conversation, where introduction or opening is natural.

exordium.etymology: Borrowed from Latin *exordium* (“beginning, commencement”), from *exōrdior* (“to begin, commence”), from *ex* (“out of, from”) + *ōrdior* (“to begin”).

senses.definition: One who expatiates.
senses.example: My uncle is a tireless expatiator on local history, and he can talk for hours about it.

core.definition: A person who speaks or writes at great length on a subject, going into much detail and wandering freely through it.

pronunciation.tip: The stress falls on SPAY, the second syllable of 'expatiate', and the final -or is a weak, reduced syllable. Keep the 'shee' sound clear, and do not say it as 'shuh'.

nuance.connotation: Neutral to slightly negative. It describes a long-winded speaker or writer, sometimes admiringly, sometimes with mild criticism.
nuance.usage_note: This is a rare word in American English, used mainly in literary criticism or formal writing about a speaker or essayist. Americans more often say someone 'rambles' or 'goes on and on' in everyday speech. Since it is uncommon, you should recognize it more than produce it.

distinctions.note: A rambler is a casual term for someone who talks aimlessly, while an expatiator goes into a subject thoroughly and at length, often with real interest.
An essayist writes short prose pieces on various topics, while an expatiator is defined by the habit of dwelling at length on a subject.

examples.everyday: My uncle is a real expatiator, so once he starts talking about baseball, you may be there for an hour.
examples.professional: In design reviews, Marcus is an expatiator who loves to explain every detail, so we set time limits for each topic.
examples.analytical: Montaigne is often described as an expatiator, wandering freely from one subject to the next while always returning to himself.

nuance.analogy: An expatiator is like a hiker who takes every side trail on a long walk, enjoying each one and returning to the main path only after exploring far and wide.
nuance.etymology: From Latin expatiari, 'to wander at large', from ex- 'out' and spatiari, 'to walk about', from spatium 'space'.
common_mistakes: Stressing the wrong syllable, such as ik-SPAT-ee-ay-ter, instead of stressing SPAY.
Confusing it with 'expatriate', which is about living in another country.

senses.definition: The state or quality of being expendable.

core.definition: The quality of being something, or someone, that can be given up or spent without serious loss.

pronunciation.tip: The primary stress falls on BIL, not on the first syllable. The final -ity is pronounced 'uh-tee' in American English.

nuance.connotation: Negative. It often reduces people to what they cost or contribute, so it can sound cold or dehumanizing.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use this word in business, military, and political writing when discussing whether people or resources can be cut. In everyday conversation people usually say 'replaceable' or 'they could easily get along without me.' The word can sound harsh if applied to people.

distinctions.note: Disposable refers to things meant to be thrown away, while expendable describes a loss accepted in pursuit of a goal.
Replaceability is a neutral term for whether someone can be substituted; expendability suggests they matter little to the outcome.

examples.everyday: I felt a real sense of expendability at that job, like they'd replace me in a week.
examples.professional: Leadership started talking about cuts, and the conversation quickly turned to the expendability of our entire QA team.
examples.analytical: Expendability is a moral category that reveals how institutions measure the worth of individuals against their usefulness.

nuance.analogy: Expendability treats a person like a paper cup: useful for one job, then tossed without a second thought.
nuance.etymology: From expendable, from expend, from Latin expendere, 'to weigh out,' with the suffix -ability.
common_mistakes: Stressing the first syllable (EX-pendability) instead of the BIL syllable.
Pronouncing the ending as 'i-tee' rather than 'uh-tee'.

senses.definition: Having experience and skill in a subject.
Experient.
senses.example: Her essay argues that religious faith is grounded in experienced reality rather than doctrine alone.

core.definition: Having a lot of practical knowledge and skill in a job or activity, built up over time through doing it.

pronunciation.tip: The stress falls on the second syllable, SPIR, and the -ienced ending is a reduced schwa plus /st/, so it sounds like 'unst' rather than 'enced'. Don't add an extra syllable after 'ee'.

nuance.connotation: Positive. It signals trust and skill and is usually a compliment, though in job ads it can feel like a stock phrase.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use it constantly in job postings ('experienced developer wanted') and in everyday talk ('an experienced driver'). It is neutral and polite. With people and things, it usually takes 'in' or 'with': 'experienced in sales' or 'experienced with Python'.

distinctions.note: 'Experienced' means you have done something for a long time; 'expert' means you are recognized as a top authority, which is a higher and rarer status.
'Skilled' focuses on ability at a task, while 'experienced' focuses on the years or repetitions behind that ability.

examples.everyday: My neighbor is an experienced gardener, so I asked her what to plant in the shady part of the yard.
examples.professional: We need an experienced engineer on this migration, someone who has already moved a database like this one.
examples.analytical: An experienced reader of Scripture learns to notice how the surrounding context changes the force of a single word.

nuance.analogy: Like a well-worn trail: the more people have walked it, the easier it is to follow, and experience is the years of walking.
nuance.etymology: From Latin experiri, 'to try, test', via Middle English experience.
common_mistakes: Saying 'experienced of' instead of 'experienced in' or 'experienced with'.
Mispronouncing it with an extra syllable, like 'ex-pee-ree-ENSED'.

senses.definition: An act of atonement for a sin or wrongdoing.

core.definition: In theology, the removal of sin or guilt by a sacrifice or act of atonement; making amends for wrongdoing.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on AY. Say four syllables: ek-spee-AY-shun. Don't confuse it with 'expiration' (ek-spuh-RAY-shun).

nuance.connotation: Serious and solemn, suggesting guilt being cleansed or paid for.
nuance.usage_note: Used in theology, literature and formal writing. In ordinary speech, Americans say 'making amends' or 'atoning'. The RSV uses 'expiation' in Romans 3:25 and 1 John 2:2.

distinctions.note: Propitiation involves appeasing anger; expiation focuses on cleansing sin or guilt.
Atonement is the wider reconciliation; expiation is the removal of guilt within it.
Expiration means ending or running out, as of a contract; it is unrelated to guilt.

examples.everyday: He saw his years of community service as a kind of expiation for what he'd done.
examples.professional: In my commentary, I explain why the RSV renders hilasterion as 'expiation' in Romans 3:25.
examples.analytical: Where expiation concerns the removal of sin, propitiation concerns the divine response, and the debate over these terms shapes doctrines of atonement.

nuance.analogy: Expiation is like washing a stain out, while propitiation is like calming a person's anger.
nuance.etymology: From Latin expiatio, from expiare, 'to atone for', from ex- plus piare, 'to appease'.
common_mistakes: Confusing 'expiation' with 'expiration' because of similar sound.
Placing stress on the first syllable.
nuance.biblical_note: The Greek hilasterion and hilasmos are rendered 'expiation' in the RSV. Romans 3:25 says God put Christ forward as an expiation by his blood, to be received by faith. 1 John 2:2 and 4:10 call Christ the expiation for our sins. In Leviticus 16, the blood on the mercy seat expiates the sins of the people.

senses.definition: The act of opening or unfolding.
senses.example: Careful explication of the folded map revealed hidden routes across the valley.

senses.definition: The sense given by an expositor.
senses.example: Her explication of the passage clarified what the commentary had obscured.

senses.definition: (dated) The act of explaining; an explanation.
senses.label: dated

core.definition: A detailed explanation or interpretation of a text, idea, or concept, especially in literary or philosophical study.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on KAY, the syllable before the -tion ending, which is pronounced shun. The first syllables are quick and reduced, so the word is not ek-SPLAY-shun.

nuance.connotation: Neutral. It suggests careful interpretive work rather than a quick answer.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use explication mainly in literature courses, philosophy, and theology, often in the phrase close explication. In everyday speech, people say explanation. The word is respected in academic settings but would sound pretentious in casual talk.

distinctions.note: Explanation is the general everyday word, while explication is a careful, detailed interpretation of meaning, usually of a text or concept.
Exegesis is a specialized term for the interpretation of Scripture, while explication applies to texts and ideas in general.

examples.everyday: My sister gave me a long explication of why the movie's ending was so sad.
examples.professional: Give me a short explication of the bias term in the design doc before the review.
examples.analytical: Her close explication of the poem's imagery reveals how grief and hope are held together in a single line.

nuance.analogy: Like a careful translation that unpacks each clause so the full meaning becomes visible.
nuance.etymology: From Latin explicatio, an unfolding or explanation, from explicare.
common_mistakes: Using explication for everyday explanations, where explanation is more natural.
Confusing explication with exegesis, which is specifically the interpretation of Scripture.

explication.etymology: Middle French *explication* and its etymon Latin *explicatio*.

senses.definition: In an explicit manner.
senses.example: The fifth amendment to the United States constitution provides explicitly for the protection of private property.

core.definition: In a clear, direct way that leaves nothing to guess.

pronunciation.tip: Stress the first syllable of the main root, SPLIS. The ending is a short 'it' followed by 'lee', and the middle syllable is not 'uh' in careful speech.

nuance.connotation: Neutral; it signals that something was said directly, which is usually helpful.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use 'explicitly' to emphasize that something was clearly stated, often in emails, contracts and instructions ('I explicitly said no'). In casual speech 'specifically' or 'exactly' is more common. It often appears in negatives like 'not explicitly stated'.

distinctions.note: Expressly is stronger and often means for a particular purpose ('made expressly for kids'); explicitly means directly stated.
Specifically narrows focus to a particular item; explicitly stresses that the statement was direct.

examples.everyday: Can you explicitly tell me what time you want me to pick you up?
examples.professional: Please explicitly list any assumptions in the model documentation so reviewers can check them.
examples.analytical: Kant explicitly rejects the claim that moral worth depends on the consequences of an action.

nuance.analogy: If 'explicit' is a sign with the words printed on it, 'explicitly' is the act of pointing directly at that sign.
nuance.etymology: Formed from explicit with the adverbial ending -ly, from Latin explicitus.
common_mistakes: Misspelling it as 'explicitely'.
Placing it awkwardly before a verb in speech; it usually goes before the verb phrase it modifies.

senses.definition: The act of expunging or erasing.
The condition of being expunged.

core.definition: The act of erasing or removing something, especially a record, so that it no longer exists or can be seen.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on SPUHNG. The final consonant k in parentheses is optional, so the ng may merge into a clean ng-sh sound, and the last syllable is a reduced shuhn.

nuance.connotation: Neutral and formal, used in legal, archival, or editorial contexts.
nuance.usage_note: Americans more often say 'expungement' for the legal removal of records. 'Expunction' is a less common, more formal variant found in some older texts and in discussions of erasure of data or history. In casual conversation, people say 'erase', 'delete', or 'clear'.

distinctions.note: Expungement is the standard American legal term for removing a criminal record; expunction is the less common, more formal word for the same general act.
Deletion is an everyday word for removing text or files; expunction suggests a formal, complete erasure from an official record.

examples.everyday: My friend said the expunction of her old college record took longer than she expected.
examples.professional: The records office confirmed the expunction of the disputed entry after the audit was closed.
examples.analytical: The historian argued that the expunction of inconvenient documents from the archive shaped how the event was remembered.

nuance.analogy: Like wiping a chalkboard clean so that no trace of the old writing remains.
nuance.etymology: From Latin expungere (to blot out), from ex- (out) and pungere (to prick, mark).
common_mistakes: Using expunction in casual speech where erase or delete is more natural.
Mixing it with expulsion, which means forcing someone out of a place or group.

senses.definition: The operation of stretching a broken bone so as to bring the fragments into the same straight line.
senses.example: The doctor applied gentle extension to the broken wrist before wrapping it in a cast.

senses.definition: The act of extending; a stretching out; enlargement in length, breadth, or time; an increase.
senses.example: Next month the house is undergoing an extension.

senses.definition: That property of a body by which it occupies a portion of space (or time, e.g. "spatiotemporal extension").
senses.example: Descartes argued that extension, not color or taste, is the essential property of physical matter.

senses.definition: A written engagement on the part of a creditor, allowing a debtor further time to pay a debt.
senses.example: The bank granted the farmer a written extension on his overdue loan until harvest season.

senses.definition: University programs that are targeted at the broader (usually adults) community whose participants are not full-time enrolled students.
senses.example: She enrolled in the university's extension program to take evening classes in data visualization.

senses.definition: The set of tuples of values that, used as arguments, satisfy the predicate.
senses.example: The logic module enumerates the extension of each predicate before running the join.

senses.definition: The state of being extended.
A short exact sequence 1→H→E→G→1, or the group E therein.
senses.example: The group theorist showed that every extension of Z by Z/2 splits in this case.

senses.definition: A short exact sequence 0→B→E→A→0, or the object E therein.
senses.example: Her homework asked us to classify every module extension of a ring by a simple module.

senses.definition: A part of a building that has been added onto the original.
senses.example: We built a sunroom extension off the back of the house for the kids' playroom.

senses.definition: An outgrowth; a part of something that extends its capabilities.
senses.example: Parents who treat their children as an extension of themselves

senses.definition: Capacity of a concept or general term to include a greater or smaller number of objects; — correlative of intension.
senses.example: Philosophers note that 'animal' has greater extension than 'dog,' though less intension.

senses.definition: Semantic widening, broadening of meaning.
senses.example: The word 'holiday' shows an extension of meaning from sacred feast to any day off.

senses.definition: An exercise in which an arm or leg is straightened against resistance.
senses.example: My physical therapist had me do knee extension exercises with a resistance band.

senses.definition: A simple offensive action, consisting of extending the weapon arm forward.
senses.example: The fencing coach taught us a quick extension, driving the front arm straight at the target.

senses.definition: A numerical code used to indicate a specific telephone in a telecommunication network.
senses.example: Call the front desk and ask for extension 214 before the meeting starts.

senses.definition: Ellipsis of file extension.
senses.example: Files with the .txt extension usually contain text.

senses.definition: An optional software component that adds functionality to an application.
senses.example: a browser extension

senses.definition: A kind of derivative morpheme applied to verbs in Bantu languages.
senses.example: In Swahili, the applicative extension on a verb lets it take an extra object.

senses.definition: The ideal in the codomain generated by the image of the given ideal under the given homomorphism.
senses.example: Compute the extension of the ideal along the homomorphism before checking primality.

senses.definition: Clipping of hair extension, nail extension, or eyelash extension.
senses.example: She booked an appointment for hair extension, adding length for her wedding day.

senses.definition: Ellipsis of extension cord.

core.definition: An additional phone line within a business or building, or an extra period of time added to a deadline or permit.

pronunciation.tip: Stress the second syllable, STEN, and say the ending as 'shun,' not 'shee-un.' The flapped t is not involved here, but the final syllable is a quick, weak schwa.

nuance.connotation: Neutral and practical. Asking for an extension is a polite request in work or school settings.
nuance.usage_note: In American offices, 'extension' almost always means a phone line within the company, so 'Can I get your extension?' means 'What is your internal phone number?' Asking for an 'extension' on a deadline is also very common in school and work, and people usually say 'Could I get an extension?' or 'Can we push the deadline?' The word is used in everyday speech for a phone line, a cord, or an add-on, so context matters.

distinctions.note: Extra time is more casual and usually refers to time added by a game or event, while extension is the formal word for an official addition to a deadline.
Addition means something added to something else, while extension more often means stretching or continuing something already there.

examples.everyday: Sure, it's extension 204, so just ask for Dana when you call.
examples.professional: I've asked the client for a two-week extension on the report deadline.
examples.analytical: In logic, the extension of a term is the set of things to which it applies, as opposed to its intension or meaning.

nuance.analogy: An extension is like adding a room onto a house: the space gets bigger, but the building stays the same.
nuance.etymology: From Latin extensio, a stretching out, from extendere.
common_mistakes: Saying 'extension' for a telephone number in general; in American offices, 'extension' usually means the internal line, not the full number.
Using 'extension' as a verb; the verb is 'extend,' as in 'extend the deadline.'

extension.etymology: From Middle English *extensioun*, from Old French *estension*, from Latin *extensiō*.

conversation.text: My extension is 4512 if you need to reach me directly.
Please dial the extension of the person you're trying to reach.
I asked my professor for an extension on the paper.

senses.definition: The action of making or becoming extinct; annihilation.
senses.example: Scientists warn that habitat loss could push many frog species toward extinction.

senses.definition: The fading of a conditioned response over time if it is not reinforced.
senses.example: After several weeks without a reward, the rats showed extinction of the lever-pressing response.

senses.definition: The absorption or scattering of electromagnetic radiation emitted by astronomical objects by intervening dust and gas before it reaches the observer.
senses.example: Astronomers corrected the brightness of the distant quasar for interstellar dust extinction.

senses.definition: The inability to perceive multiple stimuli simultaneously.
senses.example: Patients with parietal damage sometimes show extinction, failing to notice a second object.

core.definition: The complete disappearance of a species, or a state where something no longer exists, or a conditioned behavior fading away.

pronunciation.tip: Stress the second syllable, STINGK, and say the final syllable as 'shun.' Do not pronounce the 'ng' and 'k' as separate sounds with a vowel between them.

nuance.connotation: Neutral in biology and general use, but serious and somber when describing species or human life.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use 'extinction' most often for species disappearing, as in 'mass extinction' or 'faces extinction.' In psychology it means a conditioned response fading because it is no longer reinforced, a technical use Americans learn in psychology courses. In everyday talk people say 'die out' or 'disappear' when the context is less formal.

distinctions.note: Endangerment means being at risk, while extinction means the process or result of disappearing completely.
Death is the end of an individual's life, while extinction refers to a whole species or group, or to something that no longer exists.

examples.everyday: The dodo's extinction happened in the late 1600s, so you can only see one in a museum.
examples.professional: The team planned the retirement of the old API so it would not face sudden extinction.
examples.analytical: Mass extinction events mark sharp breaks in the fossil record, and scientists debate their causes.

nuance.analogy: Extinction is like the last ember in a campfire: once it stops glowing, no amount of wind brings it back.
nuance.etymology: From Latin exstinctio, a quenching or putting out, from exstinguere.
common_mistakes: Confusing 'extinction' with 'extinguishment,' which is the act of putting out a fire or ending a right.
Stressing the first syllable instead of the second.

extinction.etymology: From late Middle English, borrowed from Latin *extinctio* (“extinction, annihilation”), from *extinguere*, past participle *extinctus* (“to extinguish”); see extinguish.

senses.definition: The state or quality of being factual.
That which is factual.
senses.example: Historians separated the factuality of the diary from the author's embellishments.

core.definition: The quality of being based on facts, or of being a fact; whether a claim or report is actually true to the facts.

pronunciation.tip: The stress falls on the third syllable, AL, and the endings -i-ty are weak. Don't say 'fact-you-ALL-i-tee' with a long 'oo'; the middle syllables are quick.

nuance.connotation: Neutral. It describes a property of a statement or report without praising or criticizing it.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use factuality mainly in journalism, academic writing, philosophy and debates about media, as in 'questions of factuality.' In everyday talk, people usually say 'accuracy' or 'whether it's true.' The word is useful in writing about claims, but it can sound stiff in conversation.

distinctions.note: Accuracy is how closely something matches a standard or measurement; factuality asks whether a statement is a fact at all.
Truth is broader and often philosophical; factuality is narrower and usually refers to verifiable claims in reporting or data.

examples.everyday: My uncle keeps sharing articles, but I always wonder about their factuality before I believe them.
examples.professional: Before we publish the dashboard summary, someone needs to verify the factuality of each figure.
examples.analytical: The historian argues that the factuality of the chronicle is doubtful, since its dates conflict with independent records.

nuance.analogy: Factuality is like a bridge inspector checking whether the bridge is actually standing on solid ground, not just looking sturdy.
nuance.etymology: From fact, from Latin factum 'something done,' from facere 'to do, make.'
common_mistakes: Using factuality to mean 'accuracy' in a precise measurement context, where accuracy is the better word.
Stressing the wrong syllable as 'FAK-tu-al-i-ty' instead of stressing the 'al' syllable.

senses.definition: Being or relating to a fad; trendy.
senses.example: His faddish obsession with cold-brew coffee lasted exactly one summer before he moved on.

core.definition: Following a fad; trendy in a short-lived way, often in a shallow or unserious manner.

pronunciation.tip: Stress the first syllable and make the second syllable a short 'ish,' like the end of 'dish.' Don't add an extra syllable or stress the ending.

nuance.connotation: Mildly negative. It suggests something is trendy for a short time and not serious.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use faddish to criticize things that follow trends, such as a faddish diet or faddish language in a report. It is less polite than 'trendy,' which can sound positive. Use it when you want to suggest that something will not last.

distinctions.note: Trendy is often neutral or positive; faddish is more critical and suggests the trend is shallow or brief.
Fashionable can describe long-lasting style; faddish implies a short, intense popularity.
Faddy describes a person who is fussy about food or habits; faddish describes things that follow trends.

examples.everyday: Her new hobby is kind of faddish, but she seems to really love it.
examples.professional: The team dropped that faddish framework once the community stopped supporting it.
examples.analytical: Some critics argue that the church's faddish use of therapeutic language neglects its older theological vocabulary.

nuance.analogy: Faddish is like a sugar rush: sweet and sudden, and over before you know it.
nuance.etymology: From fad, with the suffix -ish meaning 'having the quality of.'
common_mistakes: Confusing faddish (trendy things) with faddy (fussy people).
Using faddish as a neutral compliment; Americans usually hear it as a criticism.

senses.definition: Faint of heart; irresolute; fearful.
senses.example: The fainthearted hikers turned back before the steep ridge, deciding the climb was too risky.

core.definition: Lacking courage or resolve; easily frightened or hesitant when facing difficulty or danger.

pronunciation.tip: The main stress falls on 'faint', with a lighter secondary stress on 'heart'. The 'r' in 'heart' is pronounced clearly in General American, and the final syllable is a reduced 'id'.

nuance.connotation: Negative. It criticizes a lack of courage, though it can be used teasingly among friends.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use 'fainthearted' in writing, speeches and sometimes in casual talk to describe someone who hesitates to take risks. It is written as one word or with a hyphen, and the one-word spelling is more common today. Saying it directly to someone can sound insulting, so it works best for describing situations or in a light, teasing tone.

distinctions.note: 'Timid' describes a shy or easily scared temperament, while 'fainthearted' describes a lack of courage when a challenge arises.
'Cowardly' is stronger and more moral in tone, while 'fainthearted' is milder and often used for hesitation rather than shameful behavior.

examples.everyday: Don't be fainthearted about it; just call the landlord and ask for the repair.
examples.professional: The fainthearted proposal would cut the budget by only two percent, which will not solve the underlying problem.
examples.analytical: Rather than a fainthearted retreat, Luther's stand at Worms demanded a costly and public commitment to conscience.

nuance.analogy: A fainthearted person is like a swimmer who stays near the shallow end: safe, but never reaching the deeper water.
nuance.etymology: From 'faint', meaning weak or feeble, combined with 'heart', meaning courage or spirit.
common_mistakes: Stressing both words equally, which makes the word sound clumsy; the main stress is on 'faint'.
Pronouncing the 'r' in 'heart' as silent, as some speakers do in British English; General American keeps it.

senses.definition: To exhaust the strength or endurance of, by hunger; to cause to be very hungry.
senses.example: The long delay at the border famished the travelers, who had packed only a few crackers.

senses.definition: To kill, or to cause great suffering to, by depriving or denying anything necessary.
senses.example: Cruel policies that cut off food and medicine famished entire villages during the drought.

senses.definition: To force, control, or constrain by famine.
senses.example: The siege was designed to famish the city into surrender before the spring offensive began.

senses.definition: To die of hunger; to starve to death.
senses.example: Thousands famished in the camps when the grain shipments stopped arriving in winter.

senses.definition: To suffer extreme hunger or thirst, so as to be exhausted in strength, or to nearly perish.
senses.example: After three days lost in the desert, the hikers were famishing and close to collapse.

senses.definition: To suffer extremity from deprivation of anything essential or necessary.
senses.example: Without funding, the rural clinic began to famish for supplies long before the storm arrived.

core.definition: To make someone extremely hungry, or to cause suffering through lack of food.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on the first syllable. The second syllable is short 'ish' as in 'finish', not 'eesh'. The 'a' is a short vowel as in 'hat'.

nuance.connotation: Negative. It describes severe hunger or suffering caused by deprivation.
nuance.usage_note: In everyday American speech, the verb famish is rare; people say 'starve' or 'be really hungry'. You will hear the adjective famished often, as in 'I'm famished!' for being very hungry after a long day. The verb mostly appears in literature, history and formal writing.

distinctions.note: Starve means to suffer or die from lack of food; famish is more literary and can describe making someone very hungry.
Hungry is the everyday word for wanting food; famish suggests a much more severe state.

examples.everyday: The long drought famished the village until the aid trucks finally arrived.
examples.professional: The budget cuts famished the department of the resources it needed, so the project stalled.
examples.analytical: The regime famished rural communities by seizing their grain stores, a strategy that the report describes as deliberate.

nuance.analogy: Like a plant left without water: it slowly weakens until it cannot survive.
nuance.etymology: From Old French afamer, from famine, hunger.
common_mistakes: Using 'famish' in casual conversation where 'starve' or 'I'm famished' is natural.
Saying 'famish' with a long i, as in 'fah-mish'; the vowel is short.
nuance.biblical_note: Famine is a major theme in Scripture, usually from the Hebrew ra'av, meaning hunger or famine. Genesis 12:10 describes Abram going down to Egypt because of famine in the land. Genesis 41:54-57 tells how Joseph's stored grain saved Egypt and surrounding nations during a severe famine. Lamentations 4:9 describes those who died by hunger as suffering more than those killed by the sword.

famish.etymology: From Middle English *famisshe*, from *famen* (“starve”), from Old French *afamer*, ultimately from Latin *famēs* (“hunger”).

senses.definition: A paying passenger, especially in a taxi.
Money paid for a transport ticket.
senses.example: train fare

senses.definition: Food and drink.
senses.example: The restaurant's fare was simple but delicious, with fresh bread and grilled fish.

senses.definition: Supplies for consumption or pleasure.
senses.example: The television channel tended to broadcast unremarkable downmarket fare.

senses.definition: Used to express evaluations [with adverbial complement].
senses.example: She fared badly in the accident.

senses.definition: To experience luck, fortune or treatment (of a certain kind).
senses.example: She fared badly in the accident.

senses.definition: To proceed or progress (in a certain way).
senses.example: We will continue to monitor how the hurricane fares against projected models.

senses.definition: To happen or occur (in a certain way).
senses.example: We shall see how it fares with him.

core.definition: The money a passenger pays to ride in a taxi, bus, subway, or other public transportation.

pronunciation.tip: Pronounce it as one rhotic syllable, with the r clearly sounded at the end. Don't add an extra vowel before the r, and don't confuse it with fair, which sounds the same.

nuance.connotation: Neutral. It is a practical, everyday term about cost.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use fare for the price of a ride on a bus, subway, train, or taxi. The phrase fare is a common word on transit signs and in conversations with drivers. For a taxi, people also say the fare to mean the total meter amount. Fare is not used for the price of a plane ticket in everyday speech; people say ticket price.

distinctions.note: A fee is charged for a service or permission, like a bank or license fee. A fare is specifically the payment for a ride on transportation.
A ticket is the document that proves you paid or have a right to travel. The fare is the money you pay for it.

examples.everyday: The bus fare went up to two dollars and fifty cents last month.
examples.professional: Our transit app shows the fare for each route before you book a ride.
examples.analytical: A flat fare structure makes the cost of travel independent of distance, which affects how riders from different neighborhoods are charged.

nuance.analogy: Like a toll you pay to cross a bridge, the fare is the price you pay for the ride itself.
nuance.etymology: From Old English faru, travel or journey, related to fare (verb).
common_mistakes: Using fare for the price of a plane ticket; in the US people say ticket price or airfare.
Saying fair with the same sound; fare is for transportation costs, fair means just or a festival.

fare.etymology: From Middle English *fare*, from a merger of Old English *fær* (“journey, road”) and *faru* (“journey, companions, baggage”), from Proto-Germanic **farą* and **farō* (“journey, fare”), from Proto-Indo-European **per-* (“a going, passage”).

conversation.text: The bus fare is three dollars, and you need exact change.
Do you take cards, or should I pay the fare in cash?
The cab driver picked up a fare outside the hotel.

senses.definition: A market where farmers and growers sell produce directly to the public.

core.definition: A market where local farmers and growers sell fresh fruit, vegetables, and other produce directly to shoppers, often on weekends.

pronunciation.tip: Stress the word market on its second syllable, MAR, which is the main stress, with farmers getting secondary stress. The final -et in market is a reduced vowel close to kit, and the flapped t sounds softer than a clear t.

nuance.connotation: Positive. It suggests fresh, local, healthy food and community.
nuance.usage_note: Americans often say farmers market for a weekly or seasonal outdoor market, usually on weekends. People might say they are going to the farmers market for tomatoes or flowers. Many towns also call them farmers' markets, and the apostrophe is optional. The term is common in neighborhood, parenting, and health-conscious conversation.

distinctions.note: A grocery store is a permanent indoor store that sells many kinds of food, while a farmers market is typically seasonal and sells mainly local produce directly from producers.
A flea market sells used goods and collectibles, while a farmers market sells fresh food grown by farmers.

examples.everyday: Let's go to the farmers market on Saturday morning and grab some peaches before they sell out.
examples.professional: Our company sponsors a booth at the downtown farmers market to promote the local food program.
examples.analytical: Farmers markets reshape local food systems by shortening supply chains and shifting some purchasing power from national distributors to nearby growers.

nuance.analogy: A farmers market is like a neighborhood potluck of growers: the food comes straight from the people who made it, with no middleman in between.
nuance.etymology: Farmer comes from Anglo-Norman fermer, one who holds land for rent; market comes from Latin mercatus, trade.
common_mistakes: Saying farmer market without the s; the usual American form is farmers market.
Stressing market as the only strong syllable and flattening the word; keep FAR-mers and MAR both clear.

conversation.text: The farmers market downtown is open every Saturday morning.
I bought fresh peaches and honey at the farmers market.
Bring cash to the farmers market; some vendors don't take cards.

senses.definition: Abstinence or mortification for religious reasons, especially abstinence from food.
Abstinence from food, limiting caloric intake, for medical or health reasons, dieting.
senses.example: My doctor recommended fasting for twelve hours before the blood test.

core.definition: Going without food, or certain foods, for a set time, usually for religious reasons; also abstaining from food for health reasons.

pronunciation.tip: Stress the first syllable. The vowel is the short 'a' of 'cat', and the final -ing has a short 'ih' sound, not 'eeng'.

nuance.connotation: Neutral. In religion it is positive and disciplined. In health contexts it is usually neutral and part of a trend, as in 'intermittent fasting'.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use it in two settings: religious practice (Lent, Ramadan, Yom Kippur, Orthodox fasts) and health or diet ('intermittent fasting'). 'Fasting' for a blood test means no food or drink except water beforehand. It is not a synonym for dieting.

distinctions.note: Dieting means regulating what you eat over time, usually to lose weight; fasting means not eating for a set period.
Abstinence is broader (avoiding food, drink, or other things); fasting is specifically about food.
Starving is involuntary and harmful; fasting is chosen and temporary.

examples.everyday: I can't have coffee yet because I'm fasting for my blood work this morning.
examples.professional: Our wellness program offers a seminar on the research behind intermittent fasting.
examples.analytical: In Christian ascetic writing, fasting is not mere self-denial but a discipline that frees the soul for prayer.

nuance.analogy: Fasting is like turning off the background noise so you can hear something quieter.
nuance.etymology: From Old English fæstan, 'to hold firm, to observe abstinence'.
common_mistakes: Confusing 'fast' (verb, to abstain) with 'fast' (quick).
Saying 'FAS-teen' instead of FASS-ting.
Using 'fasting' for ordinary dieting.
nuance.biblical_note: Hebrew tsom and Greek nēsteia mean abstaining from food as a sign of humility, mourning or seeking God. Joel 2:12 calls Israel to return to God with fasting, weeping and mourning. In Matthew 6:16-18 Jesus tells his followers to fast without display. Matthew 4:2 records his forty days of fasting in the wilderness.

traditions.view: Fasting is central to the church year, with long fasts such as Great Lent and weekly fasts on Wednesdays and Fridays, usually abstaining from meat, dairy, and often oil and wine. It is joined to prayer and almsgiving.
The church requires limited fasting and abstinence on days such as Ash Wednesday and Good Friday, with abstinence from meat on Fridays in Lent. Other penitential practices are encouraged.

Fasting is not required by most churches but is commended as a voluntary spiritual discipline. Practice varies widely, from regular fasts among some evangelicals and Pentecostals to little observance in other groups.

senses.definition: A list of numbers that represents one example for a model.
senses.example: Each customer record was converted into a feature vector before training the classifier.

core.definition: An ordered list of numbers representing one data example, used as the input a model reads.

pronunciation.tip: The main stress is on VEK, the first syllable of vector. Don't pronounce it as VEE-tor or with a long o; the final -or is a reduced er sound.

nuance.connotation: Neutral. It is a precise technical term with no emotional charge.
nuance.usage_note: Engineers use feature vector in machine learning code, papers, and team discussions, as in encode each user as a feature vector. In this sense, vector just means a list of numbers, though the geometric picture helps with distance calculations. Non-specialists may not know the term, so explain it if needed.

distinctions.note: An embedding is a learned, dense vector that captures meaning; a feature vector can be built by hand from raw attributes.
A feature vector is one row for one example; a feature matrix stacks many of them together.

collocations: pass the feature vector to the model

examples.everyday: Basically, the app turns each photo into a feature vector, then checks how close it is to the one saved.
examples.professional: Each customer record becomes a feature vector of twelve numbers before it goes into the classifier.
examples.analytical: Representing an example as a feature vector assumes that its relevant properties can be captured in a fixed number of coordinates.

nuance.analogy: Like a spreadsheet row where every column holds a number, and the whole row describes one person.
nuance.etymology: Feature from Old French faiture; vector from Latin vector, carrier, from vehere, to carry.
common_mistakes: Saying a feature vector for a single feature; one vector holds many features.
Mispronouncing vector with a long o or long e instead of VEK-ter.

conversation.text: Each customer is represented as a feature vector with forty numeric values.
Check that the feature vector is in the same order at training and serving time.

senses.definition: A fabrication, fantasy, invention; something fictitious.
senses.example: a figment of one's imagination

core.definition: Something invented or imagined that is not real, such as a story, idea or fantasy.

pronunciation.tip: Stress is on the first syllable. The final syllable is weak, so say 'muhnt' with a reduced vowel.

nuance.connotation: Neutral, sometimes slightly dismissive about something that seems imagined.
nuance.usage_note: Americans mostly use figment in the phrase 'a figment of your imagination,' often said playfully or to suggest that someone's worry is not real. It is common in everyday speech, though a little formal. A natural reply is 'Ha, I guess I imagined it.'

distinctions.note: Fiction is a genre or a literary work; figment is a single imagined thing or idea that does not exist.
Illusion is something that appears real but is not; figment is more about something made up by the mind.

examples.everyday: Did you really hear someone knocking, or was that just a figment of your imagination?
examples.professional: The error report looked like a real outage, but it turned out to be a figment of a misconfigured alert.
examples.analytical: For Berkeley, matter is not an independent substance but a figment of perception, sustained by the mind.

nuance.analogy: A figment is like a shadow that looks solid until you turn on the light.
nuance.etymology: From Latin fictmentum, from fingere, meaning to shape or invent.
common_mistakes: Using figment for a real story; for a made-up story, use fiction or myth.
Pronouncing it 'FIG-ment' with a long i; the i is short.

figment.etymology: From Late Latin *figmentum* (“anything made, a fiction”), from *fingō* (“make, form, feign”); see *fiction*, *feign*, *feint*.

senses.definition: A selective list of movie titles that share a similar characteristic such as the same genre, the same director, the same actor etc.
senses.example: The film club's filmography focused on heist movies, from classics to recent indie hits.

core.definition: A list of films made by a particular person, such as an actor or director, or films grouped by a theme, genre or studio.

pronunciation.tip: The main stress falls on the third syllable, MOG, not on the first. The -graphy ending reduces to 'gruh-fee', and the vowel in MOG is the 'ah' of 'cot', which Americans pronounce the same as 'caught'.

nuance.connotation: Neutral. It is a practical, descriptive term used in film studies, entertainment media and industry contexts.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use filmography for a complete or selected list of films by one person, such as an actor's full filmography on IMDb or a Wikipedia page. It can also refer to a list of films on a shared subject. When you want the list of one film's credits, say credits or cast and crew instead.

distinctions.note: A discography lists recordings, usually albums or songs by a musician; a filmography lists films.
Credits name everyone who worked on one film; a filmography lists the films one person has worked on.

examples.everyday: I looked up the actor's filmography online and realized I had seen most of his movies.
examples.professional: Before the interview, the casting team reviewed the candidate's filmography to check her range across genres.
examples.analytical: A director's filmography can reveal recurring preoccupations, so critics often read the complete body of work as a single argument.

nuance.analogy: A filmography is like a table of contents for someone's career in movies, showing each chapter they have written.
nuance.etymology: From film and the suffix -graphy, from Greek graphein, to write.
common_mistakes: Stressing the first syllable, as in FIL-mog-ra-fee.
Using filmography for the cast list of one movie, when credits is the more natural word.

senses.definition: Synonym of thumb.

core.definition: In statistics, the leftmost nonzero digit of a number, as studied in Benford's law.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on DIJ. The second syllable of 'digit' is a reduced 'it', not 'ut', and the g is the soft sound of 'j'.

nuance.connotation: Neutral. It is a precise technical term.
nuance.usage_note: In American English, 'first digit' in the sense of thumb is anatomical and rarely used; ordinary speakers say 'thumb.' In data science and statistics, 'first digit' or 'leading digit' is the common term for the leftmost nonzero digit of a number. Use it in technical contexts, such as fraud detection or auditing.

distinctions.note: Both terms name the same concept; 'leading digit' is slightly more common in formal statistics papers.
The last digit is the rightmost digit, often used for checksums or rounding; the first digit is the leftmost nonzero one.
'Thumb' is the anatomical term for the digit on the hand; 'first digit' in statistics has nothing to do with hands.

examples.everyday: My friend in finance said the first digit of those numbers was the only one she checked.
examples.professional: We'll flag any transaction whose first digit doesn't follow the expected Benford distribution.
examples.analytical: The distribution of the first digit is non-uniform, which is why Benford's law can reveal fabricated figures.

nuance.analogy: Like the first letter of a word that tells you a lot about where the word belongs, the first digit reveals a pattern in a whole set of numbers.
nuance.etymology: 'First' from Old English fyrst plus 'digit' from Latin digitus, 'finger or toe'.
common_mistakes: Pronouncing 'digit' as 'DIJ-ut', which makes the second syllable sound like a different word.
Using 'first digit' in everyday English to mean thumb, which sounds technical and unnatural.

senses.definition: The time when light first appears in the morning; dawn, especially the start of dawn.
The first use of a telescope or other instrument to capture an astronomical image.
senses.example: The team celebrated first light when the new telescope captured the nebula's first image.

core.definition: The first appearance of daylight in the morning; dawn, especially the very start of the light.

pronunciation.tip: The main stress falls on LIGHT, which sounds like 'lyte'. The first word is secondary stress, so keep the r-colored vowel clear.

nuance.connotation: Positive or neutral. It suggests a new beginning or a quiet morning.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use 'first light' in camping, hunting, fishing, and early-morning work, as in 'We leave at first light.' It is also used in astronomy and telescope work for the first image taken by an instrument. In everyday talk it is simpler and more natural than 'dawn' in planning sentences.

distinctions.note: 'Dawn' is the broader time when morning begins; 'first light' is the very first moment light is visible.
'Sunrise' is when the sun's top edge appears on the horizon, which comes after first light.
'Daybreak' is a more poetic word for the start of day; 'first light' sounds more practical.

examples.everyday: We have to leave at first light if we want to reach the trailhead before the heat.
examples.professional: The telescope will take its first light image before the end of the month.
examples.analytical: The poem's final stanza turns on first light, which marks both the end of the night and the speaker's reckoning.

nuance.analogy: Like the first crack of a window in the morning, first light lets the day in before the full brightness arrives.
nuance.etymology: 'First' from Old English fyrst plus 'light' from Old English leoht.
common_mistakes: Saying 'first light of the morning' in a redundant way when 'first light' already means morning.
Pronouncing 'light' as 'lite', which some learners do, but the American vowel is a long 'y' sound.

senses.definition: To lose excitement, to become less exciting; to end, fail or die out in a weak or disappointing way.
senses.example: The initial excitement about the startup began to fizzle out after the first year.

senses.definition: To kill or end (someone or something).
senses.example: The new regulation was designed to fizzle out the rumor before it spread.

core.definition: To lose energy or interest gradually and end weakly, or to fail to continue as expected.

pronunciation.tip: The main stress falls on 'out,' so say 'fiz-uhl OWT' with a strong emphasis on the final word. Link the words smoothly, so that 'fizzle out' sounds almost like one phrase with a light stress on fizz.

nuance.connotation: Negative. It describes a disappointing or unremarkable end, often with a sense of loss of excitement.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use fizzle out when a relationship, trend, conversation, or project slowly loses energy and stops. It is common in everyday speech and in workplace talk, for example, 'The discussion fizzled out after lunch.' A natural reply might be 'Yeah, it happens,' or 'That's too bad, we had such high hopes.'

distinctions.note: Die out suggests something disappearing completely, often over time, while fizzle out emphasizes a weak or disappointing loss of energy.
Peter out is very similar, but it sounds slightly more literary and is less common in everyday speech than fizzle out.
Fall through means a plan fails to happen at all, while fizzle out suggests it started and then slowly lost momentum.

examples.everyday: Our group chat fizzled out after everyone moved to different cities.
examples.professional: The pilot program fizzled out because nobody owned it after the first month.
examples.analytical: The movement fizzled out not through defeat but through a slow loss of shared purpose among its members.

nuance.analogy: A fizzle out is like a candle that burns lower and lower until the flame is almost gone.
nuance.etymology: Fizzle out combines fizzle, to hiss weakly, with out, meaning completely or to an end.
common_mistakes: Stressing 'fizzle' heavily and making the phrase sound like one word with the wrong rhythm.
Saying 'fizzle down' in place of 'fizzle out,' which sounds unnatural to Americans.
Using it for something that stops suddenly; 'shut down' or 'stop' would be more accurate for a sudden end.

senses.definition: Directing all one's efforts towards achieving a particular goal.
Dealing with some narrowly defined aspects of a broader phenomenon.
senses.example: The study was focused on how sleep affects memory in adults over sixty.

core.definition: Directing all of your attention and effort toward a particular goal, without being distracted.

pronunciation.tip: Stress the first syllable. The -ed is pronounced as a t because it follows the unvoiced s sound, so say FOH-kuhst, not FOH-kuhsd.

nuance.connotation: Positive. It praises determination and discipline, though it can sound narrow in some contexts.
nuance.usage_note: Americans say I'm focused or I'm trying to stay focused in everyday talk, and it often appears in workplace talk about projects and goals. A natural reply to 'You seem focused today' is 'Yeah, I'm trying to finish this report.' In research writing, focused on can also mean narrowly limited to a topic.

distinctions.note: Focused usually refers to attention aimed at a goal; concentrated is more about intense mental effort or, for substances, a high density.
Single-minded implies total devotion to one aim, sometimes to the point of ignoring everything else; focused is more neutral.

examples.everyday: I'm trying to get focused before the kids wake up.
examples.professional: The team is focused on shipping the new API by Friday.
examples.analytical: The study is focused on a small group of urban schools, so its findings may not generalize.

nuance.analogy: Like sunlight through a magnifying glass, all the energy is aimed at one small spot.
nuance.etymology: Past participle of the verb focus, from Latin focus, hearth or fireplace.
common_mistakes: Pronouncing the -ed as a separate d sound instead of t.
Saying I am focus instead of I am focused.

senses.definition: Any solid substance that can be consumed by living organisms, especially by eating, in order to sustain life.
senses.example: The innkeeper brought them food and drink.

senses.definition: A foodstuff, a type of food.
senses.example: The farmers market sells fresh local food that tastes better than anything at the supermarket.

senses.definition: Anything that nourishes or sustains.
senses.example: The man's inspiring speech gave us food for thought.

senses.definition: Any illegal substance or illegal substances, drugs.
senses.example: Dealers were moving food through the nightclub, and the bouncers looked the other way.

core.definition: Any substance that people or animals eat to get nourishment and energy.

pronunciation.tip: A single syllable with a long oo vowel, the same as in 'mood' and 'cool'. Don't add a glide, as in 'foo-ud'. The final d is a clear, released sound.

nuance.connotation: Neutral in general use. 'Good food' is positive, while 'junk food' or 'fast food' can carry a negative judgment about healthfulness.
nuance.usage_note: In everyday talk food is usually uncountable: 'We need food,' 'I love Thai food,' or 'The food here is great.' Americans say 'the food' to mean the quality of a meal at a restaurant. Use foods only when talking about types, such as in nutrition or 'processed foods.'

distinctions.note: A meal is a specific occasion of eating, such as breakfast or dinner; food is the general substance.
Foodstuff is more formal and often refers to a raw material or product category; food is the everyday word.
A dish is one prepared item; food is general and can refer to anything eaten.

examples.everyday: The food here is amazing, and the portions are huge.
examples.professional: We need to confirm the food budget before we finalize the catering order for the offsite.
examples.analytical: Food is never merely fuel; it carries memory, culture, and moral choice.

nuance.analogy: Food is like fuel for a car: without it the engine stops, and the quality of it shapes how well the engine runs.
nuance.etymology: From Old English fōda, meaning nourishment or food.
common_mistakes: Saying 'a food' or 'foods' when you mean a meal; say 'a meal', 'a dish', or 'some food'.
Writing 'I love the food' when you mean food in general; without 'the', it means food as a whole.

food.etymology: From Middle English *fode*, *foode*, from Old English *fōda* (“food”), from **fōdō*, from Proto-Germanic **fōdô* (“food”), from Proto-Indo-European **peh₂-* (“to guard, graze, feed”).

senses.definition: The impression of the foot in a soft substance such as sand or snow.
Space required by a piece of equipment.
senses.example: This computer has a smaller footprint.

senses.definition: The amount of hard drive space required for a program.
senses.example: The installer's footprint on the laptop is only eighty megabytes, so it fits easily.

senses.definition: The audit trail left by a crashed program.
senses.example: The crashed process left a footprint in the system logs that helped us find the bug.

senses.definition: A trace left behind that gives evidence of some action having occurred.
senses.example: The burglars left almost no footprint, just a smudged window latch and a missing key.

senses.definition: What a person has done before, as a profession or lifestyle, serving as a model for others.
senses.example: He is following in his father's footprints.

senses.definition: The surface space occupied by a structure.
senses.example: the footprint of a building

senses.definition: A company's geographic market presence.
senses.example: The store, which is slated to open next month, increases the company's footprint in the market to 14 locations.

senses.definition: The ecological impact of a human activity, machine, etc.
senses.example: My carbon footprint is very high.

senses.definition: Availability of a satellite from the ground.
senses.example: The satellite's footprint covers most of North America, so the signal reaches our rural county.

senses.definition: A polygon representing the shape of an item.
senses.example: building footprint

core.definition: The mark or shape a foot leaves on a soft surface such as sand, mud or snow.

pronunciation.tip: Stress the first syllable, FOOT. The final nt cluster is quick, and the r in print is strong in American speech.

nuance.connotation: Neutral in everyday use. In environmental talk, carbon footprint is neutral to negative because it signals impact.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use footprint in everyday speech for a foot mark, and in business and tech for the amount of space or resources something uses. Carbon footprint is very common in American news and corporate writing. In tech, saying a program has a small footprint means it uses little memory or disk space.

distinctions.note: A footprint is the mark left by a foot; a footstep is one step or the sound of stepping.
A track is a trail of marks left by an animal or person; a footprint is one individual impression.

examples.everyday: There were little footprints in the snow leading to the back door.
examples.professional: The new service has a smaller memory footprint, so it runs fine on our old servers.
