'Leanness' refers to having little fat in a healthy way, often used for muscle or meat, while 'thinness' can refer to a general lack of body mass or width.

examples.everyday: The ice on the pond looked dangerous because of its thinness near the edges.
examples.professional: Our test sample showed a thinness in the data for users over sixty, so we need more responses.
examples.analytical: The thinness of the textual evidence makes any firm conclusion about the author's intent difficult.

nuance.analogy: Like a sheet of paper held up to the light, thinness is how little there is between one side and the other.
nuance.etymology: From 'thin' (Old English thynne) plus the suffix '-ness', meaning the state or quality of.
common_mistakes: Pronouncing it as 'thin-ee-ness' with an extra syllable; it has only two syllables.
Using 'thinness' as a compliment about a person; say 'slim' or 'slender' instead.

thinness.etymology: From Middle English *thynnesse*, from Old English *þynnes* (“thinness, slightness of density, lack of density, tenuity, fluidity, poverty, feebleness of sight, weakness”), equivalent to *thin* + *-ness*.

senses.definition: To hurl; to release (an object) with some force from one’s hands, an apparatus, etc. so that it moves rapidly through the air.
senses.example: throw a shoe; throw a javelin

senses.definition: To eject or cause to fall off.
senses.example: the horse threw its rider

senses.definition: To move to another position or condition; to displace.
senses.example: throw the switch

senses.definition: To make (a pot) by shaping clay as it turns on a wheel.
senses.example: Every Saturday, my daughter takes a pottery class where she learns to throw bowls on a wheel.

senses.definition: To send (an error) to an exception-handling mechanism in order to interrupt normal processing.
senses.example: If the file is read-only, the method throws an invalid-operation exception.

senses.definition: To confuse or mislead.
senses.example: The deliberate red herring threw me at first.

senses.definition: To send hastily or desperately.
senses.example: Their sergeant threw the troops into pitched battle.

senses.definition: To imprison.
senses.example: The magistrate ordered the suspect to be thrown into jail.

senses.definition: To organize an event, especially a party.
senses.example: She was known for throwing the craziest parties in college.

senses.definition: To roll (a die or dice).
senses.example: Before the board game starts, Grandpa always insists on throwing the dice himself.

senses.definition: To cause a certain number on the die or dice to be shown after rolling it.
senses.example: If I throw a seven on my next roll, I can finally leave jail.

senses.definition: To discard.
senses.example: Please don't throw away the receipt until the warranty expires.

senses.definition: To lift or unbalance one’s opponent and then bring him back down to the ground, especially into a position behind the thrower.
senses.example: The wrestler managed to throw his opponent to the mat with a sudden hip move.

senses.definition: To change (one’s voice) in order to give the illusion that the voice is that of someone else, or coming from a different place.
senses.example: The ventriloquist can throw his voice so that the puppet seems to speak from the back row.

senses.definition: To show sudden emotion, especially anger.
senses.example: When the umpire ruled against us, Dad threw a fit in the stands.

senses.definition: To project or send forth.
senses.example: The old projector can throw a bright image across the entire gymnasium wall.

senses.definition: To make a shape or gesture with the hands.
senses.example: I threw scissors but she threw rock and beat me.

senses.definition: To put on hastily; to spread carelessly.
senses.example: She threw a coat over her pajamas and ran out to get the newspaper.

senses.definition: To prepare (a cocktail) by pouring liquid between shakers from a height.
senses.example: The barman taught me how to throw a cocktail.

senses.definition: To twist two or more filaments of (silk, etc.) so as to form one thread; to twist together, as singles, in a direction contrary to the twist of the singles themselves; sometimes applied to the whole class of operations by which silk is prepared for the weaver.
senses.example: The mill workers throw the raw silk filaments into strong threads before weaving.

senses.definition: To install (a bridge).
senses.example: Engineers will throw a temporary bridge across the river before the highway closes.

senses.definition: Synonym of pass.
senses.example: He threw the ball to the open receiver near the end zone.

senses.definition: To deliver.
senses.example: The mail carrier will throw the newspaper onto our porch every morning.

senses.definition: To deliver (the ball) illegally by straightening the bowling arm during delivery.
senses.example: The umpire warned the bowler to stop throwing, since his arm straightened during delivery.

senses.definition: To intentionally lose a game.
senses.example: The tennis player was accused of taking bribes to throw the match.

senses.definition: (of a game where one’s role is throwing something) To perform in a specified way in (a match).
senses.example: The pitcher threw a perfect game.

senses.definition: To select (a pitcher); to assign a pitcher to a given role (such as starter or reliever).
senses.example: The manager decided to throw the rookie as a starter this season.

senses.definition: Of animals: to give birth to (young).
senses.example: The sow will throw a litter of piglets in early spring.

senses.definition: The act of throwing something.
senses.example: With an accurate throw, he lassoed the cow.

senses.definition: A move in which one lifts or unbalances one’s opponent and then brings him down to the ground.
One’s ability to throw.
senses.example: He’s always had a pretty decent throw.

senses.definition: The distance traveled by something thrown.
senses.example: a stone's throw

senses.definition: (Can we verify this sense?) The flight of a thrown object.
A distance traveled in general; displacement.
senses.example: the throw of the piston

senses.definition: A piece of fabric used to cover a bed, sofa or other soft furnishing.
A single instance, occurrence, venture, or chance.
senses.example: Football tickets are expensive at fifty bucks a throw.

senses.definition: Any of the projections integral to a crankshaft that receive or impart cranking motion from a connecting rod or similar component.
(historical) A hand-operated lathe, especially a small lathe used by clockmakers.
senses.label: historical

core.definition: To send something through the air with a quick, forceful movement of your arm and hand, letting it go.

pronunciation.tip: It is one syllable with a voiceless th, a clear r and a long oh. Do not say 'throo' or add an extra syllable as in 'thr-oh-ah.'

nuance.connotation: Neutral; it becomes negative with 'throw up' or 'throw a fit' in informal use.
nuance.usage_note: Throw is the everyday word for sports, tossing trash or keys, and expressions like 'throw a party.' In casual speech Americans say 'throw up' for vomiting, which is informal and impolite in polite company. In baseball, a pitcher 'throws' a pitch.

distinctions.note: Toss is gentle and casual, often underhand or light; throw can be forceful and cover a longer distance.
Hurl is forceful and often angry or violent; throw is the neutral general word.
Fling suggests a wide, careless motion; throw is the general word.

examples.everyday: Can you throw me the remote? It's on the couch next to you.
examples.professional: Let's throw the draft over to legal before the Friday deadline.
examples.analytical: A single counterexample can throw an entire theory into doubt, because a universal claim fails if one exception holds.

nuance.analogy: Like skipping a stone across a pond: the force you put in decides how far it goes.
nuance.etymology: From Old English thrāwan 'to turn or twist,' a sense that later shifted to 'hurl.'
common_mistakes: Confusing the past tense 'threw' with 'through' in writing, as in 'I through it.'
Using 'throw up' in polite company for vomiting, where 'be sick' or 'vomit' is more polite.

throw.etymology: From Middle English *throwen*, *thrawen*, from Old English *þrāwan* (“to turn, twist”), from **þrāan*, from Proto-Germanic **þrēaną* (“to twist, turn”), from Proto-Indo-European **terh₁-* (“to rub, rub by twisting, twist, turn”).

senses.definition: One in a series of volumes.
A large or scholarly book.
senses.example: The professor pulled a dusty old tome from the bookshelf.

core.definition: A large, heavy, or scholarly book, or one volume in a multi-volume set.

pronunciation.tip: Stress the single syllable and use a long o like the vowel in 'tow'. It is not pronounced like 'tomb', which is toom.

nuance.connotation: Neutral to slightly humorous. It suggests a book that is long, dense, or serious, and people often use it with mild exaggeration.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use 'tome' mainly for a big, serious book, often with a joking tone about its length. In everyday talk, people say 'big book' or 'thick book'. Using it for a paperback novel sounds odd, but it is fine for a dense reference work or a long academic text.

distinctions.note: Volume is the neutral word for any book in a set, while tome emphasizes size, weight, or scholarly seriousness.
Book is the everyday word; tome is more literary and suggests a long or heavy work.

examples.everyday: My grandmother keeps a huge tome of family recipes on the kitchen shelf.
examples.professional: The vendor's report was a tome, so I read only the executive summary before the meeting.
examples.analytical: Hegel's Phenomenology is a dense tome that rewards patient rereading.

nuance.analogy: A tome is like a brick of paper: heavy, solid, and meant to be studied slowly.
nuance.etymology: From Latin tomus, from Greek tomos, meaning 'section' or 'slice', from temnein, 'to cut'.
common_mistakes: Pronouncing it like 'tomb', which is a different word with a silent b.
Using 'tome' for any ordinary book, when it usually suggests a large or scholarly one.

tome.etymology: From Middle French *tome*, from Latin *tomus* (“section of larger work”), from Ancient Greek *τόμος* (“section, roll of papyrus, volume”), from *τέμνω* (“to cut, separate”).

senses.definition: The quality or degree of being toxic.
senses.example: drug toxicity

core.definition: The degree to which a substance is poisonous or harmful to living things, or to a system such as software or a community.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on the 'sis' syllable, not on the first syllable. The 'o' is the cot vowel, pronounced like 'ah', and the final 'ty' sounds like 'tee'.

nuance.connotation: Negative. It describes harm, poisoning, or a damaging environment, and it can be metaphorical for online behavior.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use 'toxicity' in medicine, environmental science, and everyday talk about harmful workplaces or online comments. In casual speech, someone might say 'The toxicity in that group chat is awful.' In professional settings, it is often paired with a measured dose or a scale. A natural reply is 'Yeah, we should mute it for a while.'

distinctions.note: 'Toxin' names a poisonous substance, while 'toxicity' names the quality or degree of being poisonous.
'Poison' is the everyday word for something that harms or kills, while 'toxicity' is the technical or formal word for the level of harm.

examples.everyday: The town tested the lake water, and the toxicity was low enough that the beach stayed open.
examples.professional: Our content moderation model flags comments with high toxicity scores, so we review them before publishing.
examples.analytical: Toxicity is not a property of a substance alone but of the dose, the route of exposure, and the biological system affected.

nuance.analogy: Toxicity is like the strength of a medicine: the same substance can be harmless in small amounts and dangerous when the dose is too high.
nuance.etymology: From 'toxic', from Latin 'toxicus', from Greek 'toxikon', poison for arrows, with the suffix '-ity' indicating quality.
common_mistakes: Stressing the first syllable as 'TOK-si-ci-tee' instead of 'tahk-SIS-uh-tee'.
Using 'toxicity' as a countable noun in casual speech when a plural form is not standard.

senses.definition: To transfer the remains of a deceased person (such as a monarch or other important person) from one place to another; to transfer a holy relic from one shrine to another.
senses.example: The monks planned to translate the relics of the saint to a new shrine in the cathedral.

senses.definition: To transfer a bishop or other cleric from one post to another.
senses.example: The Vatican decided to translate the bishop from the rural diocese to the capital city.

senses.definition: Of a holy person or saint: to be assumed into or to rise to Heaven without bodily death; also to die and go to Heaven.
senses.example: Tradition holds that the saint was translated to heaven without dying, body and soul.

senses.definition: Senses relating to the change of information, etc. from one form to another.
senses.example: Hans translated my novel into Welsh.

senses.definition: To change spoken words or written text (of a book, document, movie, etc.) from one language to another.
senses.example: Hans translated my novel into Welsh.

senses.definition: To provide a translation of spoken words or written text in another language; to be, or be capable of being, rendered in another language.
senses.example: Hans translated for us while we were in Marrakesh.

senses.definition: To express spoken words or written text in a different (often clearer or simpler) way in the same language; to paraphrase, to rephrase, to restate.
senses.example: Could you translate that legal jargon into plain English so the tenants understand it?

senses.definition: To change (something) from one form or medium to another.
senses.example: The director faithfully translated their experiences to film.

senses.definition: To change, or be capable of being changed, from one form or medium to another.
senses.example: Excellent writing does not necessarily translate well into film.

senses.definition: To generate a chain of amino acids based on the sequence of codons in an mRNA molecule.
senses.example: The ribosome reads each codon and translates the mRNA sequence into a chain of amino acids.

senses.definition: Senses relating to a change of position.
In Euclidean geometry: to transform (a geometric figure or space) by moving every point by the same distance in a given direction.
senses.example: Translate the triangle by three units to the right, keeping its orientation and shape unchanged.

senses.definition: To map (the axes in a coordinate system) to parallel axes in another coordinate system some distance away.
senses.example: When we translate the coordinate axes, the new origin sits at the point (3, 4).

senses.definition: To entrance (“place in a trance”), to cause to lose recollection or sense.
senses.example: William was translated by the blow to the head he received, being unable to speak for the next few minutes.

senses.definition: To rearrange (a song or music) in one genre into another.
senses.example: The arranger chose to translate the folk ballad into a jazz waltz for the quartet.

senses.definition: To subject (a body) to linear motion with no rotation.
senses.example: In the physics lab, we translate the block along the track without any spin.

senses.definition: Of a body: to be subjected to linear motion with no rotation.
senses.example: On the frictionless track, the cart translates smoothly forward without rotating at all.

senses.definition: In Euclidean spaces: a set of points obtained by adding a given fixed vector to each point of a given set.
senses.example: Each translation in the group shifts every point of the shape by the same vector.

core.definition: To change words or text from one language into another while keeping the same meaning.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on the second syllable, LAYT. The s sounds like z between vowels, and the first vowel is a short a, not trans-LATE.

nuance.connotation: Neutral; it is a helpful, everyday request word.
nuance.usage_note: Americans say translate from one language into another, as in translate this into English. They also say can you translate that when someone uses jargon or slang and you need an explanation. For spoken language, people usually say interpret instead.

distinctions.note: Interpret means rendering spoken language or explaining meaning orally; translate usually refers to written text.
Convert changes a format or form; translate changes meaning from one language into another.

examples.everyday: Could you translate this menu for me? I cannot tell what the second dish is.
examples.professional: We need to translate the user manual into Spanish before the product launches.
examples.analytical: A translator must decide whether to translate the original metaphor literally or preserve its effect in the target language.

nuance.analogy: Translating is like carrying a suitcase across a border: the contents must arrive intact, even though the packaging changes.
nuance.etymology: From Latin translatus, past participle of transferre, to carry across.
common_mistakes: Saying translate me instead of translate this for me
Using translate for spoken interpreting, where interpret is the usual word
nuance.biblical_note: Scripture uses translate in an older sense of carrying someone to a new state. Behind the English is the Greek metatithēmi, meaning to transfer or remove, which Hebrews 11:5 uses for Enoch. Genesis 5:24 says Enoch walked with God and that God took him, which is the background of that Hebrews passage. Both passages describe Enoch as taken from this life without experiencing death.

translate.etymology: From Middle English *translaten* (“to transport, translate, transform”), from Anglo-Norman *translater*, from Latin *trānslātus*, perfect passive participle of *trānsferō* (“to transport, carry across, translate”).

senses.definition: Situated or lying across; side to side, relative to some defined "forward" direction; perpendicular or slanted relative to the "forward" direction; identified with movement across areas.
senses.example: The engineers added a transverse brace to stop the bridge from swaying sideways.

senses.definition: Not tangent, so that a nondegenerate angle is formed between the two things intersecting.
senses.example: In the geometry homework, the two lines are transverse rather than tangent to the circle.

senses.definition: Made at right angles to the long axis of the body.
senses.example: The surgeon made a transverse incision across the abdomen to reach the appendix.

senses.definition: Anything that is transverse or athwart, such as a road or a ship's web frame.
senses.example: The ship's transverse was cracked, so the crew reinforced it before the storm arrived.

senses.definition: The longer, or transverse, axis of an ellipse.
senses.example: The transverse of the ellipse is the longer axis, which the instructor marked in red.

senses.definition: To lie or run across; to cross.
senses.example: A new ridge road transverses the valley and links the two towns.

senses.definition: To traverse or thwart.
senses.example: The senator's amendment transversed the bill's main goals, forcing a rewrite.

senses.definition: To overturn.
senses.example: The appeals court moved to transverse the lower court's ruling last week.

senses.definition: To alter or transform.
senses.example: The chef hoped the new sauce would transverse the dish from ordinary to memorable.

core.definition: Lying or running across something, at an angle or at right angles to its main direction or length.

pronunciation.tip: The stress falls on VURS, the second syllable. Say the ur as in 'nurse' with a strong American r, and do not confuse it with 'traverse', which is a different word.

nuance.connotation: Neutral. It is a precise descriptive term.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use 'transverse' mainly in mathematics, engineering, physics and anatomy. In everyday speech, people would say 'crosswise', 'across' or 'sideways'. The word is clear in technical writing, but in conversation it can sound stiff.

distinctions.note: Perpendicular means meeting at exactly 90 degrees, while transverse means crossing at any angle across the main direction.
Horizontal means level, relative to the ground. Transverse means across something, whatever its orientation.
Longitudinal means along the length of something, while transverse means across it. The two are often paired in engineering and physics.

examples.everyday: The carpenter put a transverse beam across the doorway to hold up the wall above it.
examples.professional: The engineer says the transverse load on the bridge needs more support, so we have to revise the design.
examples.analytical: The transverse axis of an ellipse is its shorter diameter, perpendicular to the major axis, and the curve is symmetric about both.

nuance.analogy: A transverse beam is like a rung on a ladder that cuts across the two long rails.
nuance.etymology: From Latin transversus, 'turned across', the past participle of transvertere.
common_mistakes: Confusing 'transverse' with 'traverse', which is a verb meaning to cross.
Using 'transverse' for a precise 90-degree angle; it means across, and perpendicular is the exact right-angle term.

senses.definition: A tremble.
senses.example: A slight trembling in her voice gave away how nervous she really was.

core.definition: A slight, quick shaking movement, often caused by fear, cold, weakness or strong emotion.

pronunciation.tip: Stress the first syllable, and keep the bl cluster quick with a syllabic L. The final -ing is a short 'ing' sound, not 'eeng'.

nuance.connotation: Neutral to negative, depending on context. It often suggests fear, nervousness or emotion, and it can also describe tenderness or reverence.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use trembling more often as an adjective or in phrases such as 'trembling voice' or 'trembling hands'. As a noun, a tremble or a shake is more common in speech. In religious or literary writing, trembling may carry a sense of awe or reverence.

distinctions.note: Shaking is the everyday word for any shake, while trembling usually suggests small, rapid movement caused by emotion or weakness.
Tremor is a more technical word used in medicine or about earthquakes, while trembling is more common in ordinary speech.
Quivering suggests a finer, more delicate movement, often of lips or a voice, while trembling can be stronger.

examples.everyday: I could hear a trembling in his voice when he asked me for help.
examples.professional: She spoke with a trembling voice during the meeting, clearly nervous about presenting her results.
examples.analytical: In Scripture, trembling before God is often a sign of reverence for his holiness rather than mere fear.

nuance.analogy: Trembling is like a tuning fork that keeps humming after it is struck, a small motion that comes from inside.
nuance.etymology: From tremble, from Old French trembler, from Late Latin tremulare, meaning to shake.
common_mistakes: Using trembled as a past tense; the past tense of tremble is trembled, but in everyday speech Americans often say 'was trembling' or 'was shaking'.
Using trembling as a main verb without a helping verb, as in 'he trembling', which is ungrammatical.
nuance.biblical_note: The Greek word is tromos (τρόμος), meaning trembling, and the phrase 'fear and trembling' (phobos kai tromos) appears in Philippians 2:12, urging believers to work out their salvation with reverent seriousness. Psalm 2:11 calls for serving the LORD with awe and reverence. Isaiah 66:2 speaks of the person who trembles at God's word, meaning someone who takes it seriously.

senses.definition: A trigraph, a sequence of three letters representing one phoneme.
An n-gram consisting of three items from a sequence.
Any of the eight combinations of three complete or broken lines forming half of a hexagram in Chinese system of divination I Ching.
senses.example: In the I Ching, each trigram is built from three solid or broken lines stacked vertically.

core.definition: A sequence of three consecutive items, such as letters or words, used in text analysis and language modeling.

pronunciation.tip: Stress the first syllable, TRY, and pronounce gram with a short a as in 'cat.' Do not say 'TRY-gram-uh' or add a vowel after the m.

nuance.connotation: Neutral; it is a precise technical term with no emotional charge.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use trigram mainly in data science, linguistics, and natural language processing, for example in 'a trigram model.' Outside that, in Chinese culture, it refers to the eight trigrams of the I Ching, a classical divination text. People may also mistake it for trigraph, which is different.

distinctions.note: A trigraph is three letters that together represent one sound, such as 'tch,' while a trigram is any three consecutive items in a text.
A bigram is a sequence of two items, so it captures less context than a trigram but is cheaper to estimate.

examples.everyday: My phone's autocomplete is basically a trigram model, guessing my next word from the last two I typed.
examples.professional: We'll add trigram features to the text classifier and compare the F1 score against the baseline.
examples.analytical: A trigram model estimates each word from the two words before it, capturing local order while missing dependencies that span longer distances.

nuance.analogy: A trigram is like a three-bead window sliding along a string of beads: each window shows you a small patch of the pattern.
nuance.etymology: From tri- 'three' and -gram, from Greek gramma 'letter, something written.'
common_mistakes: Confusing trigram with trigraph, which refers to three letters representing a single sound.
Using trigram for any three-word phrase, when the term usually refers to counts in a corpus or model.

senses.definition: A stand with three short legs, especially for cooking over a fire.
senses.example: Set the hot casserole dish on the trivet so the table doesn't scorch.

senses.definition: A stand, sometimes with short, stumpy feet, or a mat used to support hot dishes and protect a table; a coaster.
senses.example: She placed the teapot on a cork trivet to protect the walnut table.

senses.definition: A weaver's knife used to cut out the wire that was used to form a pile.
senses.example: The weaver used a trivet to cut the wire loops that formed the carpet's pile.

core.definition: A metal or heat-resistant stand or mat set under a hot pot or dish to protect the table or counter from heat.

pronunciation.tip: Stress the first syllable, TRIV. The second syllable is a reduced vowel like it, and the final t is nearly silent before a pause. Make the v clear and do not say b.

nuance.connotation: Neutral; a plain household word.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use trivet for the pad or stand under a hot casserole dish, pot or teapot, usually on a dining table or counter. You will see it in housewares stores and recipe instructions. A cloth pad is more often called a hot pad, and a coaster is for cold glasses. A natural request is: Could you grab a trivet for the casserole?

distinctions.note: A hot pad is usually a cloth or quilted pad for holding a hot handle; a trivet is a rigid stand or mat set under a dish on the table.
A coaster protects a table from the moisture of cold drinks, not from the heat of a hot dish.

collocations: set the pot on a trivet
place a trivet under the dish

examples.everyday: Put the casserole on the trivet so it doesn't scorch the table.
examples.professional: Can someone grab a trivet for the hot dish before it damages the table at the potluck?
examples.analytical: A trivet works as a thermal barrier between the hot vessel and the table, reducing heat damage to the surface.

nuance.analogy: A trivet is a shield for the table, catching the heat before it reaches the wood.
common_mistakes: Confusing trivet with trivia or trivial; the word is trivet, with stress on TRIV.
Calling it a hot plate, which in American English means a small portable cooking burner.

trivet.etymology: From Middle English *trevet*, from Old English *trefet*, borrowed from Latin *tripēs* (“tripod”).

senses.definition: Of or relating to a truth function; having a truth value that depends solely on the truth values of its components.

core.definition: Describing a compound statement whose truth value depends only on the truth values of its component statements, not on their meaning.

pronunciation.tip: The main stress falls on FUNK in 'function', with a lighter stress on 'truth'. Americans reduce the middle syllables of 'functional' to a quick schwa, so say 'FUNGK-shuh-nuhl', not 'FUNK-shun-al'.

nuance.connotation: Neutral. It is a precise technical term with no emotional charge.
nuance.usage_note: Logicians, philosophers, and computer scientists use this word when discussing connectives like AND, OR, and NOT. Outside those fields, most Americans would not use it. In a class or paper, you might say 'the connective is truth-functional' to mean its output is fixed by its inputs.

distinctions.note: A truth-functional connective is determined only by the truth values of its parts, while an intensional context (such as 'it is necessary that') depends on more than those values.

examples.everyday: My friend said that 'if it rains, we stay in' is basically a truth-functional statement, and I had no idea what he meant.
examples.professional: Our rule engine treats each AND and OR as truth-functional, so the output depends only on the inputs.
examples.analytical: Classical propositional logic is truth-functional, which is why the material conditional is defined by its truth table alone.

nuance.analogy: A truth-functional connective is like a vending machine: the output depends only on which coins you insert, not on anything else about you.
nuance.etymology: Formed from 'truth' and 'function' with the suffix '-al'.
common_mistakes: Stressing 'functional' as FUNK-shun-AL, which sounds unnatural to Americans.
Using it to mean 'practical' or 'useful', which is a different sense.

senses.definition: An abnormal growth; differential diagnosis includes abscess, metaplasia, and neoplasia.
senses.example: a benign tumor

core.definition: An abnormal mass of tissue that forms when cells grow and multiply uncontrollably; it may be benign or malignant.

pronunciation.tip: The stress falls on the first syllable, and the second syllable is a reduced 'er' with a clear American r. Do not pronounce the second syllable as 'more.'

nuance.connotation: Negative: a tumor causes fear, though many are benign.
nuance.usage_note: Americans say tumor in medical settings, news, and everyday talk about health. The spelling 'tumour' is British, and Americans would find it unusual. Not every tumor is cancerous, so people often ask whether it is benign or malignant.

distinctions.note: A cyst is a sac filled with fluid or other material, while a tumor is a solid mass of abnormally growing cells.
Lesion is a broader term for any area of damaged or abnormal tissue, while tumor specifically refers to an abnormal growth.

examples.everyday: My dad had a small tumor removed last year, and he is doing well now.
examples.professional: The radiology report flagged a tumor in the left lung and recommended a biopsy before any treatment decision.
examples.analytical: Whether a growing mass counts as a tumor depends on whether its cell growth is uncontrolled and no longer serves the body's normal regulation.

nuance.analogy: Like a weed spreading in a garden, growing where it should not and crowding out healthy plants.
nuance.etymology: From Latin tumor, 'a swelling,' from tumere, 'to swell.'
common_mistakes: Spelling it 'tumour,' which is the British form.
Assuming every tumor is cancerous, when many are benign.

tumor.etymology: From Middle English *tumour*, from Old French *tumour*, from Latin *tumor* (“swelling”), from *tumeō* (“bulge, swell”), from Proto-Italic **tumēō*, from Proto-Indo-European **tewh₂-* (“to swell”).

senses.definition: Having two tongues; double-tongued.
senses.example: The two-tongued serpent in the children's story was a clear symbol of deceit.

senses.definition: Deceitful; lying; two-faced.
(rare) Possessing the ability to speak two languages; synonym of bilingual.
senses.example: Growing up in Montreal, she was two-tongued, fluently switching between English and French at dinner.
senses.label: rare

core.definition: Deceitful and saying different things to different people; two-faced or double-talking.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on the second part, and the word ends in the cluster ng then d, so do not add a vowel between them. Say tongue as 'tung', not 'tong'.

nuance.connotation: Negative: it accuses someone of dishonest speech.
nuance.usage_note: Americans rarely use two-tongued in everyday talk; they say two-faced, double-talking or lying instead. It appears mostly in literary writing, sermons and Bible translations, where it describes a person who speaks deceitfully. In casual conversation it may sound stiff or old-fashioned, though it can work in a formal speech about dishonesty.

distinctions.note: The everyday American equivalent for deceit; two-tongued is more literary and focuses on speech.
A near synonym with the same meaning; both are formal, but double-tongued appears more often in writing.
Two-tongued once meant speaking two languages, but that sense is rare and archaic; bilingual is the normal word.

examples.everyday: A guy that two-tongued is hard to trust, because he tells everyone what they want to hear.
examples.professional: In a performance review, avoid two-tongued feedback; praising someone in private and criticizing them in public destroys trust.
examples.analytical: The prophetic critique of two-tongued leaders shows that deception in speech corrupts a community, since words are the shared basis of trust.

nuance.analogy: Like a road sign pointing in two directions at once, two-tongued speech leaves the listener lost.
nuance.etymology: From two and tongued, with tongue meaning speech or language.
common_mistakes: Assuming it means bilingual, which is an outdated sense.
Pronouncing tongued as tong-ed with a separate syllable.
nuance.biblical_note: 1 Timothy 3:8 (RSV) says deacons must not be double-tongued, meaning they should not tell one story to one person and a different story to another; the Greek word is dilogos, meaning saying two things or speaking double. The RSV uses double-tongued, a close equivalent of two-tongued, and the passage links this trait with sincerity in the office of deacon.

two-tongued.etymology: From Middle English *two-tounged*, *two tungyd*, equivalent to *two* + *tongued*.

senses.definition: Having two wheels; birotate.

core.definition: Having two wheels, such as a bicycle, motorcycle or scooter.

pronunciation.tip: Stress the first part, as in any compound.

nuance.connotation: Neutral and descriptive, with no positive or negative charge.
nuance.usage_note: Americans describe bicycles and motorcycles as two-wheeled vehicles, but in everyday speech they more often say bike, bicycle or motorcycle. In conversation the noun 'two-wheeler' is more common than the adjective. It appears most in product descriptions, news and transport planning.

distinctions.note: A noun for a bicycle or motorcycle, used in conversation. Two-wheeled is the adjective that describes the vehicle.
A narrower term for a pedal-powered two-wheeled vehicle. Two-wheeled is broader and covers motorcycles and scooters too.

examples.everyday: We rented two-wheeled scooters to ride along the beach path.
examples.professional: Our fleet analysis separates two-wheeled deliveries from car deliveries because their routes and costs differ.
examples.analytical: The stability of a two-wheeled vehicle depends on continuous balance rather than on a fixed base of support.

nuance.analogy: Like a tightrope walker's pole, it stays upright only through constant small corrections.
nuance.etymology: From two and wheel, with wheel from Old English hweol.
common_mistakes: Pronouncing 'wheeled' like 'wild'; the vowel is a long 'ee'.
Using the adjective as a noun, instead of saying 'two-wheeler' in conversation.

senses.definition: A typographical error.
senses.example: Sorry, I meant to say “buy a SODA”—“sofa” was a typo.

senses.definition: (dated) A compositor; a typographer.
senses.example: The newspaper's veteran typo could set a full page of type in under an hour.
senses.label: dated

senses.definition: To make a typographical error.
senses.example: I typoed the client's name in the email, so I sent a correction.

core.definition: A small mistake in typed or printed text, such as a wrong letter, a missing word, or a misspelling caused by a slip.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on the first syllable, and the final 'o' is a long 'oh' sound. Do not shorten it to 'tuh-pə', and do not confuse it with 'typical', which has a different stress and ending.

nuance.connotation: Mildly negative but forgiving; it is usually said with a shrug or apology.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use 'typo' constantly in texts, emails and casual talk, as in 'Sorry, that's a typo.' In formal writing, use 'typographical error' or simply 'error'. The verb 'to typo' is informal and rare, so 'I made a typo' is the natural phrase.

distinctions.note: A misspelling comes from not knowing the correct spelling; a typo is an accidental key slip, even when the writer knows the word.
Error is a general word for any mistake; typo is specific to a wrong character or word in typed text.
A misprint is an error in printed material; a typo can occur in any typed text, including emails and messages.

examples.everyday: Sorry, that's a typo, I meant to say Thursday, not Tuesday.
examples.professional: I caught a typo in the subject line before the email went out to the whole team.
examples.analytical: A typo is an error of execution rather than of knowledge, which is why careful writers often miss it on rereading.

nuance.analogy: A typo is like a loose letter on a sign: the meaning is usually clear, but it catches the eye.
nuance.etymology: Short for typographical error, from Greek typos 'impression' and graphein 'to write'.
common_mistakes: Writing the plural as 'typoes'; the correct plural is 'typos'.
Using 'typo' for a grammar mistake; it refers to a slip in typing or spelling.

senses.definition: Not surveyed or mapped.

core.definition: Not surveyed or mapped; unknown and not yet explored, so that you cannot be sure what lies ahead.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on the second syllable, CHAR. The first syllable is a weak schwa, so do not say a strong 'un'. The final -ed is a short 'id' sound.

nuance.connotation: Neutral to slightly exciting; it describes unknown ground, which can be thrilling or risky depending on context.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use 'uncharted' literally for maps and figuratively for anything new, from a business strategy to a life stage. It often appears in news and business talk, such as 'uncharted waters for the company'. It is more common in writing and speech about change than in casual small talk.

distinctions.note: Unexplored means no one has visited the place; uncharted specifically means it has not been mapped, even if people may have been there.
Unknown is general and covers anything you do not know; uncharted suggests a space or path with no map or guide.

examples.everyday: Retiring early and moving abroad is uncharted territory for us, but we're excited.
examples.professional: Launching a product in the European market is uncharted territory for our team, so we need a clear plan.
examples.analytical: Quantum computing raises ethical questions that remain largely uncharted in current moral philosophy.

nuance.analogy: An uncharted island is like a blank page on a map: the land is there, but nobody has drawn it yet.
nuance.etymology: From un- (not) + charted, from chart, from Latin charta, a sheet of papyrus or paper.
common_mistakes: Misspelling it as 'uncharter' or 'unchartered'; the correct spelling is uncharted.
Using 'uncharted' for things that are simply new without any sense of unknown risk, which can sound overdramatic in casual talk.

senses.definition: The characteristic of being uncouth.

core.definition: The quality of being rough, unrefined or lacking good manners and social polish.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on KOOTH, the same as in uncouth. The final -ness is a reduced schwa, so it sounds like nuhss, not a long e sound.

nuance.connotation: Negative: it names a lack of refinement and can sound critical of someone's character or manners.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use uncouthness when discussing manners, character or style in an essay, review or formal comment. In everyday speech they would more often say bad manners or crudeness. It is rarely used in daily conversation.

distinctions.note: Rudeness is a specific act of disrespect; uncouthness is a more general lack of refinement that may be harmless.
Vulgarity suggests coarse or offensive language or content; uncouthness covers awkward manners more broadly.

examples.professional: The hiring panel noted an uncouthness in his email tone that did not suit our client-facing team.
examples.analytical: Critics argued that the novel's uncouthness was a deliberate rejection of the polished manners expected in that period.

nuance.analogy: Like rough edges on unfinished wood: the piece works, but the surface has not been sanded smooth by good manners.
nuance.etymology: From uncouth plus the suffix -ness, which forms nouns from adjectives.
common_mistakes: Pronouncing the ending as a full ness vowel; the last syllable is a reduced schwa.
Confusing uncouthness with rudeness, which refers to a specific act rather than a general quality.

senses.definition: Not found; undiscovered.
senses.example: The leak remained undetected for months because nobody checked the logs.

core.definition: Not discovered or noticed, even though it may have happened or existed for some time.

pronunciation.tip: The stress falls on TEK. The final '-ed' is pronounced as a short 'id' sound because it follows the 't' sound, so the word ends in 'tid' rather than 'tekt.'

nuance.connotation: Neutral to negative, depending on the context. It often suggests that something harmful or illegal has gone unnoticed.
nuance.usage_note: Americans often use 'undetected' in the phrase 'go undetected' or 'remain undetected,' especially for errors, diseases, crimes, and bugs. In everyday talk, people usually say 'nobody noticed' or 'slipped by.' The word sounds natural in news reports and workplace discussions.

distinctions.note: 'Undiscovered' often refers to something that has never been found, such as a planet or a species; 'undetected' often refers to something that is already there but has gone unnoticed.
'Unnoticed' is a general word for something that passes without attention; 'undetected' carries more of a sense of a hidden problem or threat.

examples.everyday: The raccoon got into the trash and went undetected until the morning.
examples.professional: The bug slipped through review and went undetected for three releases.
examples.analytical: A crime that remains undetected still raises the question of what we owe to victims we never learn about.

nuance.analogy: Like a small crack in a dam that nobody has inspected, an undetected problem may grow quietly until someone finally notices it.
nuance.etymology: From un- (not) plus 'detected,' from Latin 'detegere' (to uncover).
common_mistakes: Saying 'undetectable' when you mean 'went unnoticed'; the phrase 'went undetected' is the standard form.
Pronouncing the ending as 'tect'; the final syllable is 'tid.'

senses.definition: That undulates, or that causes undulations.
senses.example: The undulatory motion of the snake across the sand fascinated the children.

core.definition: Moving in a wavelike way, or having a smooth rising and falling pattern.

pronunciation.tip: The stress falls on UN, and the middle syllables are weak and quick. The final -ory ends in a light ee sound, not a full ory.

nuance.connotation: Neutral and descriptive. It is precise and often used in science or literary description.
nuance.usage_note: Americans rarely use undulatory in everyday speech. It appears mainly in science writing, such as biology or physics, to describe wave-like motion like a snake's movement. In general writing, wavy or undulating is more natural.

distinctions.note: Undulating is the common everyday adjective for wavy or rolling, while undulatory is more technical and less common.
Wavy is the simple everyday word, while undulatory suggests a formal or scientific description of a smooth wave pattern.

examples.everyday: That snake moved in a smooth undulatory way across the path.
examples.professional: The fish's undulatory swimming motion is easy to model with a simple wave equation.
examples.analytical: Her description of the verse has an undulatory quality, rising and falling with each line.

nuance.analogy: Like a snake moving across the sand, its body making smooth waves from head to tail.
nuance.etymology: From undulate, from Latin undulatus, from undula, a little wave, from unda, a wave.
common_mistakes: Confusing undulatory with undulating; the first is technical, while the second is common in everyday English.
Stressing the middle syllable, as in un-duh-LAY-tor-ee; the stress is on UN.

senses.definition: The characteristic of being unfit or ill-suited.
senses.example: The judge questioned the unfitness of the guardian to raise the child.

senses.definition: The characteristic of being unfit or out of physical shape.
senses.example: The judge questioned the unfitness of the guardian to raise the child.

core.definition: The state of not being physically healthy or in good shape, or of lacking the qualities needed for a role or responsibility.

pronunciation.tip: The stress is on FIT. The final -ness is a weak, reduced syllable, close to 'nus,' not a clear 'nes.'

nuance.connotation: Negative. It names a deficiency, so it can sound judgmental when used about a person.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use 'unfitness' mostly in formal, medical, military, or legal contexts, such as 'unfitness for service' or 'evidence of unfitness.' In everyday conversation, people say 'out of shape' or 'not in good condition.' Using 'unfitness' about a friend's body would sound clinical and rude.

distinctions.note: Unhealthiness refers to conditions that harm health, such as diet or environment, while unfitness refers to lacking physical conditioning or suitability.
Inadequacy means a shortfall in amount or quality, while unfitness stresses a lack of suitability for a particular role or standard.

examples.everyday: My doctor said my blood pressure is high, but she thinks the real problem is general unfitness from years of sitting.
examples.professional: HR flagged the candidate's unfitness for the role, citing a lack of experience with production systems.
examples.analytical: Locke's argument hinges on the claim that a person's unfitness for reasoning is a matter of disposition, not merely of age or circumstance.

nuance.analogy: Unfitness is like a rusty tool: it still exists and looks like a tool, but it cannot do the job it was made for.
nuance.etymology: Formed from unfit plus the suffix -ness, from Old English -nes, a noun-forming suffix.
common_mistakes: Pronouncing the final syllable as a full 'nes' sound; it should be a reduced, weak 'nus.'
Using 'unfitness' casually about someone's exercise habits; 'out of shape' sounds more natural.

senses.definition: United into a whole.
senses.example: The country finally became a unified nation after decades of regional conflict.

senses.definition: That operates as a single entity.
senses.example: Our company now runs a unified billing system across all three subsidiaries.

senses.definition: That serves all grade levels between kindergarten and twelfth grade.
senses.example: The district's unified program serves students from kindergarten through twelfth grade.

core.definition: Joined into one whole, or operating as a single system rather than separate parts.

pronunciation.tip: The main stress falls on the first syllable, YOO. The -ified ending is one syllable, 'fyde,' with the final d clearly voiced.

nuance.connotation: Positive. It suggests cohesion, teamwork and efficiency.
nuance.usage_note: Americans often use this word for a group that acts together, such as a unified front, or for a system that works as one, such as a unified dashboard. It appears in US school district names like Unified School District, which serve all grades from kindergarten through twelfth grade. In casual talk people often say 'on the same page' or 'working together' instead.

distinctions.note: United stresses people or groups joining with shared goals, as in 'united we stand'; unified stresses that something has been made into one whole or system.
Integrated emphasizes parts that work together in an interconnected way; unified emphasizes a single identity or entity.

examples.everyday: Our whole family showed a unified front when Grandpa asked us to move in with him.
examples.professional: We need a unified dashboard so every team sees the same numbers before the quarterly review.
examples.analytical: A unified account of the self must explain how memory and perception belong to a single subject.

nuance.analogy: A unified team is like a rowing crew: many people pull separately, but the boat moves forward only when they pull together in one rhythm.
nuance.etymology: From unify, from Latin unificare, from unus (one) and facere (to make).
common_mistakes: Using 'unified' and 'united' as if they were always interchangeable; 'united' is more common for people, 'unified' for systems or messages.
Stressing the second syllable, saying 'yoo-NOO-fyde' instead of YOO.

senses.definition: A distinctive outfit that serves to identify members of a group, company, prison inmates, etc.
senses.example: The security guards wore a bright orange uniform that made them easy to spot.

senses.definition: A uniformed police officer (as opposed to a detective).
senses.example: The uniform at the corner waved me over after I ran the red light.

senses.definition: In OpenGL, a global shader variable whose value does not change between rendering calls, serving as a parameter.
senses.example: In the fragment shader, the uniform stores the light color, which stays the same for every draw call.

senses.definition: Unvarying; all the same.
senses.example: Every brick in the wall was cut to the same uniform size.

senses.definition: Consistent; conforming to one standard.
senses.example: Our team applies a uniform set of rules to every project we review.

senses.definition: With speed of convergence not depending on choice of function argument; as in uniform continuity, uniform convergence.
senses.example: The theorem requires uniform convergence, so the sequence must approach its limit at the same rate everywhere.

senses.definition: (of a polyhedron) That is isogonal and whose faces are regular polygons; (of an n-dimensional (n>3) polytope) that is isogonal and whose bounding (n-1)-dimensional facets are uniform polytopes.
senses.example: A uniform polyhedron has identical vertices and faces made of regular polygons, like the truncated icosahedron.

senses.definition: Composed of a single macromolecular species.
senses.example: After repeated purification, the polymer sample was uniform and contained only one macromolecular species.

senses.definition: To clothe in a uniform.
senses.example: The school uniforms its students in navy blazers and gray slacks every morning.

core.definition: A distinctive set of clothes worn by members of a group, such as police officers, soldiers, nurses or students, to show their identity or role.

pronunciation.tip: The stress falls on the first syllable, YOO. The middle syllables are quick and reduced, and the final r is pronounced clearly in American English.

nuance.connotation: Neutral; it can suggest order, identity and discipline, or conformity and loss of individuality, depending on context.
nuance.usage_note: Americans say uniform for clothing worn by workers, students, soldiers and athletes; 'police uniform' is also common. In everyday speech, a police officer in uniform is a patrol officer, while a plainclothes officer is a detective. Note that 'uniform' in the sense of the same for everyone is also common.

distinctions.note: A uniform is worn to show a job or membership, while a costume is worn for play, parties or performance.
Outfit is a general word for any set of clothes, while uniform specifically means required, standard clothing for a group.

examples.everyday: My daughter has to wear a navy uniform to school every day.
examples.professional: Our new hires get a company uniform for the warehouse floor, so safety teams can spot them quickly.
examples.analytical: The sociologist argued that the uniform erases visible difference while reinforcing the authority of the institution.

nuance.analogy: A uniform is like a team jersey: it tells everyone at a glance which side you are on.
nuance.etymology: From Latin 'uniformis', meaning 'of one form', from 'unus' (one) and 'forma' (form).
common_mistakes: Pronouncing it as 'you-NIF-orm' with the stress in the middle; the stress is on the first syllable.
Using 'uniform' for ordinary clothes, when Americans say 'dress code' or 'work clothes' for those.

senses.definition: Done by one side only.
Affecting only one side of the body.
senses.example: The stroke caused unilateral weakness, so she could only move her left arm.

senses.definition: Binding or affecting one party only.
senses.example: The judge's unilateral decision to cancel the contract angered both companies.

core.definition: Done or decided by one side or party alone, without the agreement or participation of others.

pronunciation.tip: The primary stress falls on LAT. The t between vowels is a flap, so it sounds like a quick 'd', and the final syllables are reduced.

nuance.connotation: Neutral to negative; it often suggests a decision made without consultation or against others' wishes.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use unilateral mainly in politics, diplomacy, law and business, as in 'unilateral action' or 'unilateral decision'. In casual talk they would say 'on their own' or 'without asking anyone'. Its opposite, bilateral or multilateral, appears in the same contexts.

distinctions.note: Independent means not controlled by others, while unilateral specifically means one side acted without the agreement of the other side.
Bilateral means involving two sides together, the opposite of unilateral.

examples.everyday: My landlord made a unilateral decision to raise the rent without talking to us.
examples.professional: The manager made a unilateral change to the schedule, so the team was not consulted.
examples.analytical: The author argues that unilateral moral claims undermine the trust needed for a shared community.

nuance.analogy: A unilateral decision is like one player changing the rules of a game in the middle of play, without the other players agreeing.
nuance.etymology: From Latin 'unilateralis', from 'unus' (one) and 'latus' (side).
common_mistakes: Using 'unilateral' for a one-sided feeling; it describes actions or decisions, not personal opinions.
Stressing the wrong syllable, as in 'yoo-nih-lah-TAIR-uhl'.

unilateral.etymology: A modern creation (circa 1802), from New Latin *ūnilaterālis* (“one-sided”), from Latin *ūnus* (“one”) + *laterālis* (“sided, lateral”), equivalent to *uni-* + *lateral*.

senses.definition: Having, or operating in, a single mode.
Having a single mode (local maximum).

core.definition: Having a single mode, meaning one peak or most frequent value, as in a probability distribution.

pronunciation.tip: The primary stress falls on MOH, with a lighter secondary stress on the first syllable. The -al ending is a reduced 'dul' sound, not a full 'al'.

nuance.connotation: Neutral and purely technical, with no emotional tone.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use 'unimodal' in statistics, data science and signal processing, for example to describe a histogram with one clear peak. It is not used in everyday English, where people would say 'one peak' or 'one hump'. In data work, it is often paired with bimodal or multimodal when comparing distributions. Check your audience before using it.

distinctions.note: Bimodal means having exactly two modes or peaks; unimodal means exactly one.
Multimodal means having several modes or peaks; unimodal has only one. In other fields, multimodal can also refer to several kinds of data or communication.
Unimodular is a matrix term meaning the determinant is plus or minus one; it has nothing to do with distributions, so do not confuse them.

examples.everyday: When my friend asked about the chart, I told her the commute times had one big peak, which statisticians call unimodal.
examples.professional: The residuals look unimodal and roughly symmetric, so a normal approximation should be reasonable.
examples.analytical: A unimodal prior encodes a single most plausible value, but it may understate uncertainty when the true parameter could plausibly lie in more than one region.

nuance.analogy: A unimodal distribution is like a mountain range with a single summit: everything rises to one peak and then falls away.
nuance.etymology: From Latin uni- 'one' plus modal, from Latin modus 'measure, manner'.
common_mistakes: Confusing unimodal with unimodular, a matrix term; the two words share a prefix but mean different things.
Stressing the middle syllable of the word; say yoo-nih-MOH-dul with the main stress on MOH.

senses.definition: Being the only one of its kind; unequaled, unparalleled or unmatched.
senses.example: Every person has a unique life, therefore every person has a unique journey.

senses.definition: Of a feature, such that only one holder has it.
senses.example: The company holds a unique patent on the battery design, so rivals must license it.

senses.definition: Particular, characteristic.
senses.example: The festival has a unique atmosphere that visitors remember for years.

senses.definition: Rare or unusual.
senses.example: Finding a snowstorm in July is unique, even for a town this far north.

senses.definition: A thing without a like; something unequaled or unparalleled; one of a kind.
senses.example: Her grandmother's hand-painted teapot is a unique, and she would never sell it.

core.definition: Being the only one of its kind; unlike anything else and not equaled or matched by anything else.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on the second syllable, 'NEEK'. Start with a clear 'y' glide, as in 'you', and do not say 'oo-nick' with a short vowel.

nuance.connotation: Positive. It suggests something special, although it is sometimes overused in advertising and everyday speech.
nuance.usage_note: Strictly, 'unique' means one of a kind, so many Americans consider 'very unique' or 'more unique' wrong, though 'pretty unique' is used informally. When people want to say rare or unusual, they often use 'one of a kind' or 'unusual' instead. A natural reply when someone says 'That's unique' is 'Yeah, I've never seen anything like it.'

distinctions.note: Rare means seldom found, but there may be many examples; unique means there is only one.
Unusual means different from the normal or usual; unique means having no equal at all.
Singular is more formal or literary and can mean unique or distinguished; in grammar it means one, not many.

examples.everyday: Their pizza has a unique flavor that you won't find anywhere else in town.
examples.professional: Each customer record needs a unique identifier so we can join the two tables without duplicates.
examples.analytical: Each human life is unique before God, and theology must take that particularity seriously rather than reducing persons to types.

nuance.analogy: Like a fingerprint: many things look alike, but there is only one that is yours.
nuance.etymology: From Latin unicus, single or only, from unus, one.
common_mistakes: Saying 'very unique' or 'more unique' in careful writing, since 'unique' already means one of a kind.
Pronouncing it as 'OO-nik' with a short vowel, instead of 'yoo-NEEK'.

senses.definition: The act by which something is unloaded.

core.definition: The act or process of removing cargo, goods or passengers from a vehicle, ship, plane or container.

pronunciation.tip: The stress is on LOH, and the un- is a quick uh. The -ing ending is /ɪŋ/, a clear ng sound with the g silent.

nuance.connotation: Neutral in logistics and shipping; informal when used figuratively, as in 'unload on someone', to vent feelings.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use 'unloading' for cargo from trucks, ships and planes, as in 'the unloading dock'. In casual speech, 'I need to unload' means you want to share a problem or vent, and listeners will often ask what is wrong. For bags and groceries, Americans say 'unpacking' or 'taking the stuff out of the car'.

distinctions.note: Unpacking means taking things out of bags, boxes or suitcases you carry personally; unloading means removing cargo from a vehicle or container.
Discharge is more formal and technical, used for liquids, waste, patients leaving a hospital or ships releasing cargo; unloading is the everyday word for goods.

examples.everyday: We spent the whole afternoon unloading the groceries from the car after the big warehouse run.
examples.professional: Unloading the container takes about two hours, so let's schedule the dock crew before the carrier arrives.
examples.analytical: The economics of unloading goods at a port depend on how quickly labor, cranes and storage capacity can work together.

nuance.analogy: Like the reverse of packing a suitcase: the hard part is getting everything in, but unloading shows what you really brought.
nuance.etymology: Gerund of unload, from un- (reversing an action) plus load.
common_mistakes: Saying 'unloading' for unpacking a suitcase at home; Americans say 'unpacking' for personal bags.
Stressing the first syllable as UN-loading; the stress belongs on LOH.

senses.definition: Unfortunate, marked by misfortune.
senses.example: We were unlucky to lose the final game by a single point.

senses.definition: Inauspicious.
senses.example: Many sailors considered Friday the thirteenth an unlucky day to set out.

senses.definition: Having ill luck.
Bringing ill luck.
Mischievous.
senses.example: Her unlucky grin told me she had hidden my car keys again.

core.definition: Having bad luck, or bringing misfortune; said of people, events, or things thought to bring bad luck.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on LUHK, and the un- is a quick uh. The final -y is ee. The vowel in LUHK is short, not the long oo sound.

nuance.connotation: Negative about the situation, but often sympathetic when said to someone who had bad luck.
nuance.usage_note: Americans say 'unlucky' about people and events: 'You're unlucky; the game got rained out.' Many Americans avoid the number 13 for superstitious reasons, so you may hear 'unlucky thirteen' and see hotels skip a 13th floor. As a reply to bad news, 'That's unlucky' or 'Tough break' is natural and sympathetic.

distinctions.note: Unfortunate is more formal and sympathetic, often used for outcomes; unlucky is everyday and focuses on chance or a person's fate.
Luckless is literary and suggests a long string of bad luck; unlucky can describe a single bad moment.
Unlikely is a prediction that something will probably not happen; unlucky describes bad luck that has already occurred.

examples.everyday: Tough break, man. You were really unlucky with that flat tire on the way to the game.
examples.professional: We were unlucky with the timing: the server crashed the same afternoon the client asked for the report.
examples.analytical: Some outcomes are unlucky rather than unfair, and any theory of justice must distinguish bad luck from bad choices.

nuance.analogy: Like a traffic light turning red the moment you arrive: nothing you did caused it, but the timing is bad.
nuance.etymology: From un- (not) plus lucky, from luck, from Middle Dutch gheluc.
common_mistakes: Stressing the second syllable as un-LOO-kee; the vowel is short uh, and the stress falls on LUHK.
Using 'unlucky' to predict the future, as in 'It is unlucky it will rain'; say 'unlikely' for a prediction.

senses.definition: Not reserved: not otherwise or already committed.
senses.example: an unreserved forest

senses.definition: Not booked in advance: with no reservation.
senses.example: an unreserved table

senses.definition: Without reserve: unrestrained, unconstrained.
senses.example: an unreserved demeanor

core.definition: Complete and wholehearted, with no hidden doubts, limits or holding back.

pronunciation.tip: The stress falls on ZURVD, and the final -ed is pronounced as a plain /d/. Do not say the stress on the first syllable of 'reserve' as RE-zerv, and keep the r sound in the middle.

nuance.connotation: Positive when describing support, praise or apology. Negative when describing criticism that is harsh and unrestrained.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use this word for strong support, praise or apologies, as in 'unreserved support.' It is also common in restaurants and events to mean seats that are not assigned or booked in advance. In casual speech, people often use 'totally' or 'full' instead, but 'unreserved' sounds sincere and polished.

distinctions.note: Wholehearted is warmer and more emotional, while unreserved is more formal and suggests there are no conditions at all.
Reserved means shy or cautious in manner, which is the opposite of an open, unreserved attitude.
Unqualified suggests support without conditions and is often used in formal or professional contexts, similar in meaning to unreserved.

examples.everyday: You're welcome to stay with us, and that's an unreserved invitation.
examples.professional: She gave the proposal her unreserved support in the meeting, and the rest of the team followed.
examples.analytical: Kant's moral law demands unreserved assent, with no exception for inclination or self-interest.

nuance.analogy: Like a door that is wide open rather than just cracked, an unreserved attitude holds nothing back.
nuance.etymology: From un- plus reserved, from Latin reservare 'to keep back, save.'
common_mistakes: Confusing 'unreserved' (wholehearted) with 'reserved' (shy or cautious), which is the opposite.
Using 'unreserved' to mean 'not reserved in advance' without making it clear, which can confuse people at restaurants.

senses.definition: Unspoken.
senses.example: We discussed the terms, but the methods were left unsaid.

core.definition: Not spoken aloud; left unexpressed, though sometimes understood by the people involved.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on SAID, which rhymes with red. Do not pronounce said with a long a as in sayd.

nuance.connotation: Neutral: it can describe tension, respect, or regret depending on context.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use unsaid for feelings or agreements that everyone understands without being stated, as in an unsaid rule. It often appears in phrases such as leave it unsaid or some things go unsaid. In casual speech people say unspoken more often, though both are common.

distinctions.note: Unspoken is nearly identical and more common in everyday speech; unsaid is often used for something held back or regretted.
Unwritten refers to rules or traditions not recorded in writing; unsaid refers to things not spoken aloud.

examples.everyday: There's an unsaid rule in this office that you don't eat at your desk.
examples.professional: The hiring manager's concerns were unsaid, but everyone in the room knew the budget was the issue.
examples.analytical: Levinas argues that the saying in speech always exceeds the said, leaving an unsaid remainder.

nuance.analogy: Like the words left in a letter that was never sent, the meaning is present but not delivered.
nuance.etymology: From un- plus said, from Old English sæd, the past participle of say.
common_mistakes: Pronouncing said with a long a, as in sayd; the vowel is short like red.
Using unsaid to mean unknown; it means not spoken aloud.

senses.definition: Not selective; open and inclusive.

core.definition: Not selective; accepting or including anyone or anything without making careful distinctions or choices.

pronunciation.tip: The stress is on LEK, and the second syllable is a reduced schwa, not 'see'. End with a short -tiv, not -tive.

nuance.connotation: Neutral; it describes a lack of filtering. It can sound positive (open to all) or negative (indiscriminate), depending on context.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use this word mainly in technical, academic or policy writing about admissions, sampling or breeding. In medicine and science the standard term is nonselective, so use that in those fields. In casual speech people say 'not picky' or 'open to everyone' instead.

distinctions.note: Nonselective is the standard technical term in medicine, biology and statistics; unselective is more common in general or evaluative writing.
Inclusive stresses welcoming people on purpose; unselective stresses the absence of choosing or filtering, and can sound negative.

examples.everyday: My brother is pretty unselective about music, so he'll listen to almost anything.
examples.professional: Our recruiting pool was unselective, so we ended up interviewing far too many candidates.
examples.analytical: An unselective pedagogy that admits every student regardless of preparation raises hard questions about what learning actually means.

nuance.analogy: An unselective net catches everything that swims by, fish and debris alike.
nuance.etymology: From un- (not) plus selective, from Latin selectus, 'chosen', from seligere, 'to choose'.
common_mistakes: Using unselective to mean careless or random; it means failing to choose or filter, not carelessness.
Using it in medical or scientific writing where nonselective is the standard term.

senses.definition: Not thankful; ungrateful.
senses.example: After all we did for him, he was unthankful and never even sent a card.

core.definition: Not expressing gratitude; failing to recognize or appreciate a kindness, gift or blessing.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on THANK, and the th is voiceless as in 'thin'. The final -ful reduces to 'fuhl' and is not pronounced 'fool'.

nuance.connotation: Negative; it implies a failure of good manners or moral virtue.
nuance.usage_note: Americans usually say ungrateful in everyday talk. Unthankful is older and mostly appears in religious writing, sermons and Bible translations, so a modern speaker may sound oddly formal. A parent would more naturally say 'You're not even grateful' than 'You're so unthankful.'

distinctions.note: Ungrateful is the everyday American word for not appreciating kindness; unthankful is older and more literary.
Thankless describes a task that earns no thanks; unthankful describes a person who fails to give thanks.

examples.everyday: Don't be unthankful; your grandmother spent all day cooking for you, so say thank you.
examples.professional: The leadership seemed unthankful toward the staff who worked through the holidays to finish the release.
examples.analytical: The prophets condemn an unthankful people who forget the gifts of God and turn to other gods.

nuance.analogy: Like a guest who eats the whole dinner and leaves without a word.
nuance.etymology: From un- plus thankful, from Old English thancful, from thanc, thanks.
common_mistakes: Using unthankful as a synonym for ungrateful in everyday talk, where ungrateful is standard
Confusing it with thankless, which describes a task that earns no thanks
nuance.biblical_note: Greek acharistos (ungrateful). Luke 6:35 says God is kind even to the ungrateful and the wicked, showing that divine mercy reaches those who do not thank him. 2 Timothy 3:2 lists being ungrateful among the marks of people in the last days, alongside self-love and pride.

unthankful.etymology: From Middle English *unthankful*, from Old English *unþancful*, *unþancfull*, *unġeþancfull* (“unthankful, ungrateful”), equivalent to *un* + *thankful*.

senses.definition: Not giving the truth; providing untrue facts; lying.
senses.example: The witness was untruthful about where he had been that night, and the detective knew it.

senses.definition: Pertaining to falsehood; corrupt; dishonest.
senses.example: The senator's untruthful dealings with the lobbyists eventually ended his political career.

core.definition: Not telling the truth; saying things that are false, often deliberately.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on TROOTH, and the -ful ending is weak, pronounced with a reduced vowel, not as the full word full. The th is voiceless, as in truth.

nuance.connotation: Negative; it criticizes a person's honesty, usually in a firm or formal way.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use it for people who lie or give false information, often in formal or official contexts, as in the witness was untruthful. In casual talk people more often say dishonest or they're not telling the truth. It can sound like a firm, slightly formal criticism.

distinctions.note: Dishonest is broader and covers cheating, stealing and deceit; untruthful focuses on not telling the truth in speech or answers.
Untrue describes a statement that is false; untruthful describes a person who does not tell the truth.
Lying is the act of knowingly saying something false; untruthful describes a quality or habit and is more formal.

examples.everyday: My son was untruthful about finishing his homework, so I checked it myself.
examples.professional: If a candidate is untruthful on a résumé, the company usually has grounds to withdraw the offer.
examples.analytical: Some ethicists argue that an untruthful person harms others even when the falsehood seems minor, because it weakens the shared trust that social life needs.

nuance.analogy: Being untruthful is like a tour guide who gives wrong directions on purpose: you can still follow the guide, but you will end up lost.
nuance.etymology: From un- (not) + truthful, from truth + -ful (full of).
common_mistakes: Confusing untruthful with untrue; a person is untruthful, while a statement is untrue.
Saying untrueful; the correct adjective is untruthful.

senses.definition: The characteristic or condition of being unworthy.
senses.example: He wrestled with a deep sense of unworthiness after the scandal, doubting he deserved his old friends.

core.definition: The state of not deserving something, or lacking the qualities that merit respect, honor, or a particular status.

pronunciation.tip: The stress falls on WUR, and the th is voiced. The ending -iness is a weak 'nus' sound, not a strong 'ness' with an e.

nuance.connotation: Negative when it describes a moral or social failing; in religious contexts it can express humility before God.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use this noun in religious settings, serious conversation, and literary writing about self-worth or moral standing. In everyday talk they usually say 'I don't deserve it' or 'I'm not good enough.' In church it is common to hear a sense of unworthiness expressed in prayer, and it is usually sincere rather than insulting.

distinctions.note: Inadequacy means lacking the ability or quality for a task; unworthiness means lacking merit or moral standing.
Humility is a virtue of modest self-view; unworthiness is a feeling or condition of not deserving, which humility may acknowledge.

examples.everyday: I still struggle with a feeling of unworthiness whenever my friends praise my cooking.
examples.professional: Her performance review addressed the unworthiness of the project's final deliverable compared to its original scope.
examples.analytical: Luther's account of justification answers the conscience troubled by its own unworthiness before God.

nuance.analogy: Like a coin that is too light for the machine, unworthiness means failing the standard that others use to judge value.
nuance.etymology: From un- (not) plus worthiness, from worthy, from Old English weorth, meaning worth or value.
common_mistakes: Misspelling it as 'unworthyness'; the adjective is unworthy, so the noun takes -iness.
Using it for lack of skill; say 'inadequacy' or 'incompetence' when you mean ability.
nuance.biblical_note: Scripture often pictures people confessing their unworthiness before God, and the Greek word axios, meaning worthy, is the root of the idea. In the RSV Luke 7:6 the centurion says he is not worthy to have Jesus come under his roof. Luke 15:19 has the prodigal son confess that he is no longer worthy to be called his father's son. Genesis 32:10 records Jacob acknowledging that he is not worthy of God's steadfast love and faithfulness.

traditions.view: Orthodox liturgy includes confession of unworthiness before Communion, and the faithful are taught that the grace of God makes them worthy in a way they could not earn.
Catholics pray the centurion's words before receiving Communion, and they teach that grace, sacramental preparation, and a state of grace make reception fitting.

Protestants generally teach that believers are declared righteous by grace through faith, so unworthiness is acknowledged while worthiness is received in Christ, with Lutheran and Reformed emphasis on justification and Baptist emphasis on personal faith.

unworthiness.etymology: From Middle English *unworthynesse*; equivalent to *unworthy* + *-ness* or *un-* + *worthiness*.

senses.definition: The highest or uppermost side or portion of something.
senses.example: Climbers reached the upside of the ridge just before the storm rolled in.

senses.definition: A favorable aspect of something that also has an unfavorable aspect.
An upward tendency, especially in a financial market etc.
senses.example: Analysts say the upside for tech stocks remains strong despite rising interest rates.

senses.definition: On the top of.
senses.example: She balanced the vase upside the stack of books.

core.definition: A favorable aspect or advantage of something that also has some drawbacks, or the potential for gain in an investment or situation.

pronunciation.tip: Stress the first syllable and make it one compound word. Don't split it into two stresses like 'UP-SIDE.'

nuance.connotation: Positive, since it highlights benefits, though the phrase often appears in discussions of risks too.
nuance.usage_note: Americans often say 'the upside is...' when weighing pros and cons in a meeting or planning talk, usually followed by 'the downside.' The word is used most in business, finance, and everyday decisions. The preposition sense ('on the top of') is rare and mostly obsolete in American speech.

distinctions.note: 'Advantage' is a general benefit, while 'upside' specifically contrasts with a 'downside' in a trade-off.
'Benefit' is neutral and direct; 'upside' is more casual and often used in pairs.

examples.everyday: The upside of moving to Denver is the mountains, but the winters are brutal.
examples.professional: The upside of switching to the new vendor is a twenty percent cost reduction, though the downside is a three-week transition period.
examples.analytical: The upside of a utilitarian calculation is its clarity, but its downside is that it can justify harms to minorities.

nuance.analogy: Like the bright side of a coin that you see first when you flip it over.
